articles.title: Jack-Up Barge Strengthens Offshore Fleet with 354-Person Support Unit
articles.summary: Dutch-based Jack-Up Barge, backed by the Van Es Group, has expanded its fleet with the three-legged accommodation and services jack-up unit JB 121, following a naming ceremony in Dalian, China.The ceremony took place on November 3 at Dalian Shipbuilding Offshore…
articles.body: Jack-Up Barge Strengthens Offshore Fleet with 354-Person Support Unit Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 3, 2026 JB 121 jack-up unit (Credit: Jack-Up Barge) Dutch-based Jack-Up Barge, backed by the Van Es Group, has expanded its fleet with the three-legged accommodation and services jack-up unit JB 121, following a naming ceremony in Dalian, China. The ceremony took place on November 3 at Dalian Shipbuilding Offshore, ahead of the unit's scheduled departure for the Netherlands in early November. Jack-Up Barge, a company that provides support services across the offshore wind, oil and gas, and maritime infrastructure sectors, initiated the acquisition of JB 121 earlier in 2026 as part of its fleet expansion strategy, adding to its existing units JB 114, JB 115, JB 117 and JB 120. The new jack-up is designed to support offshore installation, commissioning, maintenance and accommodation campaigns, including offshore wind projects. Based on the GustoMSC AJ-series design, JB 121 features three truss legs with a rack-and-pinion jacking system and accommodation capacity for up to 354 personnel. The unit is equipped with a 200-tonne working load limit (WLL) main crane mounted on a cantilever, alongside two 50-tonne WLL auxiliary cranes. It also provides approximately 1,340 square meters of deck space for offshore operations. “JB 121 represents an important strategic addition to our fleet- The combination of extensive accommodation capacity, deep-water capability and offshore crane support allows us support larger and increasingly complex offshore projects, particularly within the offshore wind sector,” said Frank Kees, Managing Director of Jack-Up Barge.

articles.title: KONGSBERG expands underwater surveillance technology for port security
articles.summary: KONGSBERG has launched two new sonar systems designed to improve underwater surveillance, navigation and the protection of critical maritime infrastructure. The Norwegian technology group introduced the Aegir17 and Aegir57N, expanding its Aegir Subsea Situational Awareness (SSA) family to three commercially available...
articles.body: KONGSBERG has launched two new sonar systems designed to improve underwater surveillance, navigation and the protection of critical maritime infrastructure. The Norwegian technology group introduced the Aegir17 and Aegir57N, expanding its Aegir Subsea Situational Awareness (SSA) family to three commercially available models. The systems are intended for applications including port security, fixed maritime installations and uncrewed surface vessels. They build on sonar technology originally developed for commercial maritime operations. The expansion follows the introduction of the first Aegir SSA model, Aegir57, at ONS 2026 in August. According to KONGSBERG, all three systems are now available to order, with the first commercial Aegir delivery scheduled for November. New sonar systems extend underwater monitoring capabilities The Aegir17 is designed for long-range underwater surveillance, providing 360-degree coverage for larger maritime platforms. Its lower acoustic frequency and larger transducer offer greater detection range and definition compared with the existing Aegir57. Meanwhile, the Aegir57N combines navigation and security functions in a compact system. It directs acoustic beams towards selected areas to provide detailed information about underwater obstacles, the water column and the seabed. The system can also support navigation in poorly charted waters. Its compact design and Ethernet interface allow integration with uncrewed vessels and fixed monitoring installations. The existing Aegir57 offers 360-degree underwater detection at ranges of up to 2,000 metres. It is designed for smaller vessels, buoys and fixed installations that require continuous monitoring. KONGSBERG advances AI-powered sonar operations Alongside the product expansion, KONGSBERG is extending its collaboration with US-based automation company Viam to develop an AI-powered virtual sonar operator. The technology is intended to automatically detect and track underwater objects, reducing the need for continuous manual monitoring. It is being developed particularly for uncrewed vessels and remote installations, where operators may need to monitor several locations simultaneously. Eliot Horowitz, Founder and CEO of Viam, said the system aims to turn continuous sonar data into actionable information that allows operators to focus on detections requiring further investigation. The project builds on the companies’ earlier Sonar AI collaboration for Simrad systems, which uses automated detection technology in commercial fishing applications. According to KONGSBERG, the expanded Aegir family forms part of a broader maritime surveillance approach that combines underwater sensors with coastal radar, satellite monitoring, drone detection and autonomous underwater vehicles. While the three sonar models are available for commercial orders, the AI-powered virtual operator remains under development.

Decisions determining their anticipation or anxiety when answers are received. Those dates and decisions are also occurring after releasing this editorial opinion. For us to predict how these decisions will fall is likely compared to a Tarot Card reading or a visit to a Voodoo priestess. After all this is New Orleans. With “filming & production” underway and anticipating the movie release, let’s provide this opinion as a “trailer”. The Department of Homeland Security issued a “Jones Act” waiver on March 17, 2026. The longest and broadest waiver of the Act since the end of World War II. We believe this to be a lead topic of discussion at the maritime show in Louisiana, considering the current extension is listed to expire on November 15, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. The “end” provided that energy products included in the waiver are loaded prior to the expiration date and time. Foreign flag voyages & cargo moved during the waiver is reaching over 400 voyages and millions of barrels of petroleum distributed. A strong indication the market is important to the US Flag and commerce. Future inventories and movements will be affected despite a new extension announced or not as we enter into the winter season. A rush to load cargo prior to midnight of the end date will occur. Cargo will be delivered by foreign flag after November 15. Consider this discussion as the opening scene of the “trailer” on December 1. Question if the show opens with a group photo of roughly four thousand cheering the Department of Homeland Security announcement that the waiver has ended and no further extensions will be issued by the Administration. Or will the announcement extend the waiver into another period? A follow-on extension will result in a call for a moment of silence in New Orleans signaling the possible loss of 90,000 American seafaring jobs, and adding thousands of lost employment opportunities in shipbuilding and port operations. All occurring during the year of “Maritime Dominance”. With that thought let’s remember trailers never give up the movie ending. We intend to arrive as “extras” with balloons and the hope to celebrate the end of the extensions, followed by support of the Flag and coastal registry in the Ships for America Act. Give us a chance to be included in the photo opportunity. That said we will also look for a speaking part in the production with the simple message that the “Jones Act” debate needs to be fixed by addressing the cost to build and the future ability to renew our coastal fleets. Subsidize our commercial shipyards if the intent is to support US commercial shipbuilding. If the US shipyard elects to build for defense, let them enjoy the government support that market has been provided for decades. Defense aside, the selected commercial shipyards should enjoy their own support and join the Far East and European yards we are so anxious to compete with. They are heavily subsidized and their reported cost of delivery into the market does not reflect their government support. China does not build at the price advertised. The solution in the coastal market should not be the orchestrated elimination of selected commodity sectors within the registry while separate political decisions favor others trading outside of “energy” and protected in the same legislation. The problem is cost to build not the market. US commercial shipbuilding has been the discussion of the 2026 year. Back of the envelope calculations show over one trillion dollars of new projects in defense spending providing surface & subsurface tonnage, autonomous warfare and drones. Warfare and defense shipbuilding has changed. Requirements to address more than several warfronts have identified the need to protect both our national security and global trade with new technology. Let our Navy and Military industrial base take precedence and build to meet those requirements. US commercial shipbuilding will need take a back seat to that effort for now based upon shipyard “capacity” issues alone. And “capacity” is not only the number of qualified shipyards or graving docks. It addresses our supply chain and labor issues also. That said, defense taking the lead and the 2027 Defense Act funding will raise discussions of how that funding is distributed. The first opening projects have been issued to a single shipyard, with new ownership prior to the award, and determined by a single VCM government contract source. Historically, protests and GAO audits have been the largest issue of military industrial base delays. There is no intention for us to pack our bags with candles and stand in silence listening to a rumored end of the Jones Act, the failure of coastal registered vessels flying the flag or the delay in commercial shipyard support. In fact, with several other crucial “energy” decisions affecting the industry, it is our opinion, the Administration would benefit announcing NO FURTHER WAIVERS OR EXTENSIONS will be issued prior to the opening day in New Orleans while they contend with another crucial date of November 3rd. An announcement offered in the trailer by the lead actor or director in the production? Maybe so. However, movie trailers rarely announce a huge turn of events prior to release of the movie. What is equally important to the development of energy in the coastal trades is another decision allowing sanctioned Russian diesel oil delivered into the US market. National news has reported three vessels departing Russian refinery terminals and one of the three arriving November 7 in New York and New Jersey. A second tanker reported arriving in Houston and a third arriving, with the most disturbing of news, into Norfolk. Our largest U.S. Navy homeport and shipbuilding center on the East Coast. The foreign owner of the third vessel quickly reporting the vessel, port and cargo carried was misinformation as the ship was carrying fertilizer not diesel oil. A smart move considering merchant vessels maintaining their regulatory requirements and 1900 sanctioned vessels ignoring them have been attacked, damaged and with those damages considered a constructive total loss. Misinformation aside, the U.S. Treasury Department has issued a temporary general license bypassing aspects of the 2022 Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act and our opinion ignoring National Security. Can the trailer lead us to the true story? The answer is being discussed in New Orleans as Maritime domain awareness. AIS disruption and the concern of 1900 sanctioned “ghost” vessels entering new levels of cyber & National security concerns. The latest technology presented by Quartermaster AI with live demonstrations introducing its SmartMast technology and collection of data mapping the world’s oceans at Workboat during the show. The global security problem has also gathered a new audience as dockworkers around the world called a strike effort on Friday October 30, 2026. An action reported at 113 ports & terminals in 22 countries. Our US west coast ports with the ILWU included. The strike and walkout being advertised as an effort against the militarization of ports and shipments of war-related cargo and tagged as “Dockworkers do not work for war”. Rising living costs, and wages were also presented during the “strike” as a result of geopolitical issues worldwide. Has the trailer identified the good guys and the bad guys the final production will produce? It certainly has the ability to go beyond a drama and into an action film. Let’s hope the film does not become the “Good, the Bad and the Ugly”. Unfortunately, this is no joking matter as all of the issues waiting for positive decisions are raising costs and disrupting US and global trade. More importantly, seafarers are losing their lives and little commercial industry effort is developing to provide protection of vessel and crew. See you in New Orleans. Bring balloons.

articles.title: War Widens in the Black Sea in a Test of NATO Red Lines
articles.summary: After seven strikes on cargo ships near NATO members Romania and Bulgaria last month, the US-led military alliance said it would deploy maritime patrol aircraft, radars and drones to bolster its eastern flank in the Black Sea.

The ship sank after being hit by naval drones in the Black Sea off Bulgaria on Wednesday, according to the Bulgarian government, while en route from Haifa in Israel to Constanta in Romania. French Armed Forces/Handout via REUTERS By Tom Balmforth and Luiza Ilie LONDON/BUCHAREST, Nov 3 (Reuters) – After seven strikes on cargo ships near NATO members Romania and Bulgaria last month, the US-led military alliance said it would deploy maritime patrol aircraft, radars and drones to bolster its eastern flank in the Black Sea. Three days later, on October 23, another ship was struck just outside Romanian waters. And last week a Greek container ship was sunk by naval drones in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. Unabating attacks show how the escalating maritime war between Russia and Ukraine is expanding into a major challenge for NATO in the Black Sea that has left littoral member states such as Romania and Bulgaria exposed. Military analysts said they had little doubt that these were Russian attacks. A naval drone seen on video of the last strike resembled a Russian variant , according to shipping security firm Ambrey. “I think it’s undeniably an escalation,” said Sidharth Kaushal, a senior fellow at the London-based RUSI think-tank. Russia denies targeting Ukraine’s neighbors with drones and says that European governments are the ones escalating the war in Ukraine by supplying military aid. Russia’s defense ministry did not respond to a request for comment for this article. ANALYST SAYS RUSSIA IS TESTING RED LINES Many of the ships hit in October were anchored near or sailing to or from a key Romanian canal used by Ukraine for exports. One was in Romanian territorial waters, while the other eight were in its or Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. Iulia Joja, director of the Black Sea program for the Washington-based Middle East Institute think-tank, said Russia’s attacks were taking into account the West’s aversion to escalation. “This is about testing these red lines, with full awareness that we will do everything possible to take the most minimal measures,” Joja said, drawing a comparison with Russian drone incursions into NATO airspace in recent years. A NATO official said Russian actions aimed at dissuading NATO allies from supporting Ukraine were a serious security threat and that the alliance’s commitment to defending all its members, including those on the Black Sea, was “ironclad.” The official said there was a clear need for cost-effective counter-drone capabilities, but that the alliance had already committed to investing more than $40 billion in counter-drone capabilities in the next five years. BLACK SEA IS CRUCIAL WATERWAY For Romania, the Black Sea is a crucial waterway for trade and home to its offshore Neptun Deep project that will make it the European Union’s largest gas producer next year. Neptun Deep was approached by a naval drone in August. Bucharest has accused Russia of “systematic” strikes on civilian ships but stopped short of attributing individual attacks, citing the need for forensic evidence. Sofia has not blamed Russia, but said some of the attacks seem to benefit it. The strikes come at a time when Washington is reassessing its military presence in Europe as it focuses on China. The US withdrew 1,000 troops from Romania last year. “It’s a moment in the transatlantic relationship that Putin likely wants to use,” said a senior Romanian official. “The EU and NATO’s attention is important and their forces are currently focusing towards the north and the Baltics.” While NATO has reinforced its “enhanced forward presence” for the Baltics and Poland, Joja said it had not done the same in Romania despite Bucharest’s requests. “Brussels and Washington still don’t seem to have decided whether the Black Sea is fully part of the NATO commitment.” The Romanian official highlighted Romania’s pressing need for surface-to-air interceptors and radar systems to counter threats. Joja said the limited availability of cheap interceptor weapons, exacerbated by the war in Iran, was a central problem for the West. NEARLY 400 VESSELS HIT IN PAST YEAR The surge in strikes on Black Sea shipping has strangled a major conduit for exports of grain and oil used by Russia and Ukraine. The two sides hit 317 merchant and other vessels in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov between May and October, a more than fourfold rise on the 74 vessels they struck in the previous half-year, according to Tomas Alexa, a senior analyst at Ambrey Analytics. The tempo of attacks has fluctuated ahead of the fifth anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February. Ukraine carried out 137 attacks on ships compared with 92 Russian ones in the third quarter, while in October, Russia hit 38 compared with 5 Ukrainian strikes, Ambrey said. GRAIN EXPORTS FROM UKRAINE AND RUSSIA SLUMP Ports have been battered and exports have shriveled , forcing Russia and Ukraine to seek alternative export routes . Russia exported just 0.3 million metric tons of grain in September through the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, down from 4.74 million metric tons in the same month last year, according to Russian export data seen by Reuters. Ukraine suspended operations at its Black Sea ports in late July due to Russian attacks, prompting it to divert volumes to river ports on the Danube and onwards through Romania’s Sulina Canal and southwards through Romania’s section of the Black Sea. Even with this alternative route, Ukraine’s port exports of grain slumped to 0.81 million metric tons in September compared with 2.1 million in September last year, government data showed. Further reducing these volumes remains Russia’s primary goal with testing NATO as the secondary objective, said Andriy Ryzhenko, a naval analyst and former senior Ukrainian naval officer. ZELENSKIY WARNS OF FOOD CRISIS Last week’s attack took place as the defense ministers and military chiefs of Romania, Bulgaria and fellow NATO littoral state Turkey met in Sofia to discuss the situation. The defense minister of Turkey, which is waiting for a response from Moscow and Kyiv on a narrow maritime ceasefire proposal , used the meeting to warn Russia and Ukraine against further attacks. Turkey controls the transit of warships through the Bosphorus and Dardanelles under the Montreux Convention. Several countries, including Egypt, Turkey and India, have pushed for maritime ceasefires to avert fallout from the disruption of shipping at a time when global fuel and grain prices have soared. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday there was growing international interest in a limited ceasefire. Russia has rejected the idea of a narrow maritime ceasefire that it says would provide respite to Kyiv. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy has sounded the alarm. “Everyone is talking about diesel and forgetting about grain. In a month or two, everyone will start talking about an agricultural crisis,” he said last month. articles.title: Shell rakes in $1.45 billion for shedding its stake in Australian gas and LNG project
articles.summary: As Shell heads for the exit, ADNOC’s XRG is buying a stake in a Woodside-operated LNG and gas development in Western Australia.
articles.body: Business & Finance November 3, 2026 · 3 minutes ago Shell rakes in $1.45 billion for shedding its stake in Australian gas and LNG project As Shell heads for the exit, ADNOC’s XRG is buying a stake in a Woodside-operated LNG and gas development in Western Australia. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Karratha gas plant (NWS project) Courtesy of Woodside In a bid to optimize its Australian portfolio, Shell Australia, a wholly owned subsidiary of the UK-headquartered Shell, has struck a deal to divest its interest in a gas and liquefied natural gas (LNG) project with XRG, a subsidiary of Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), which includes Abu Dhabi Development Holding Company (ADQ) and global investment firm Carlyle. Shell has signed an agreement to sell its 16.67% non-operated interest in the North West Shelf (NWS) project to wholly owned subsidiaries of XRG for a base consideration of $1.45 billion, subject to customary adjustments, plus an additional milestone-linked contingent payment. This project comprises interconnected joint ventures involving Woodside, Chevron, BP, Shell, MIMI, and CNOOC. Related Articles Fossil Energy Woodside’s Australian gas project gets green light for 40 more years of operation 2 min read The transaction, which has an effective date of January 1, 2026, is expected to close in 2027, subject to several conditions precedent, including regulatory approvals. Shell’s 16.67% interest entails associated upstream interests, pipeline, and midstream infrastructure. The firm’s interest also covers varying participating interests in related petroleum and pipeline titles, project agreements, offtake arrangements, NWS project companies, and CNOOC-related joint ventures. This sale follows Shell’s divestment of its interest in the Browse project, a proposed offshore gas development whose concept involves piping gas from the Browse Basin to Karratha for processing and export through existing NWS infrastructure. Related Articles Authorities & Government Australia’s ‘largest untapped’ conventional gas resource gets significant project status 2 min read Given that declining production from the original NWS fields has created capacity at the project’s Karratha gas plant , plans were put in motion to extend the life of the project with the North West Shelf Project Extension using existing infrastructure so that it can continue to support local and global energy security, as well as regional development opportunities in Western Australia. " This agreement reflects our commitment to disciplined capital allocation and portfolio choices. The sale realises value from a mature, non-operated asset and supports Shell’s strategy by focusing investment on advantaged integrated gas positions, as NWS transitions in the future towards a third-party toll-processing model. We are proud of the role we played as a founding partner in NWS and the role NWS has in turn played in Western Australia. " — Cederic Cremers Shell’s Integrated Gas President Shell continues to invest in LNG and integrated gas globally and will grow LNG sales by 4-5% per year to 2030. The company, which maintains a strong presence in Australia, where it operates the Shell QGC project and Prelude FLNG, is developing the Crux project and is a joint venture partner in Arrow Energy and Gorgon. articles.title: DP crews are the new bottleneck: how OSV operators can staff vessels faster
articles.summary: I spent my early career as a deck officer in the merchant fleet, and one lesson from those years has stayed with me through almost two decades of...
articles.body: Branded Content November 3, 2026 · 1 minute ago DP crews are the new bottleneck: how OSV operators can staff vessels faster Written in partnership with Marine MAN 11 minutes read LinkedIn X Email By Pavel Manchenko, Founder and Managing Director, Marine MAN @Marine MAN / jobmarineman.com I spent my early career as a deck officer in the merchant fleet, and one lesson from those years has stayed with me through almost two decades of running a crewing company: a ship is only as good as the people on board. For offshore support vessel operators today, the scarcest resource is often not the vessel but the people who run it. Charter rates, fleet utilisation and newbuilding plans dominate the headlines, yet ask any marine superintendent what keeps them awake and the answer is usually closer to home: who will relieve the Chief Officer on the PSV next month, and does he have enough DP hours to keep his certificate valid? A platform supply vessel, an anchor handler or a construction support vessel on charter earns nothing while it waits for a qualified relief. Every crew change that slips puts pressure on the next one, stretches contracts beyond what seafarers agreed to, and eventually shows up in client audits and incident reports. In a market where skilled offshore crews are in demand across oil and gas, offshore wind and subsea construction, the operators that win are those who treat crewing as a core operational process rather than an administrative afterthought. In this article I look at why offshore crews are so hard to replace, what a late crew change really costs, and six practices that, in our experience at Marine MAN, help operators staff their vessels faster and keep them staffed. Why offshore crews are harder to replace On paper, an officer is an officer. An STCW certificate of competency is the same document whether it was earned on a bulk carrier or an anchor-handling tug. In practice, offshore operations demand a layer of skills that deep-sea trades rarely provide. Dynamic positioning is the most obvious example. A DP operator needs not only formal training but also a documented amount of sea time on DP vessels to obtain the certificate and then keep it. An officer who spends a year on conventional tonnage can find that his DP qualification has quietly lapsed. That makes the pool of officers who are both certified and current much smaller than the headline number of DP certificates suggests. Anchor handling is another. Working on deck during anchor handling and towing operations is high-risk work, and the confidence to do it safely comes from experience under a competent master and bosun, not from a classroom. The same applies to cargo operations alongside installations, where everyone on board must understand exclusion zones, weather limits and communication protocols with the platform. Then there are the clients. Oil majors, national oil companies and offshore contractors audit crew competence before a vessel goes on hire and periodically during the charter. They look at matrices of certificates, sea time on similar vessel types and DP class, and often require a minimum number of years of offshore experience for senior positions. A candidate with an excellent deep-sea record may simply not pass the client's vetting. The result is that a good officer from the merchant fleet is rarely a like-for-like replacement on an OSV. When a DP-critical position falls vacant at short notice, the real choice is often between a handful of suitable candidates, many of whom are already on board other vessels. What a late crew change really costs The direct cost is easy to see. A vessel that cannot sail because a key officer is missing goes off hire or risks penalties under the charter party. Even a single lost day can cost more than a year of crewing fees for that position. The indirect costs are less visible but just as real. When a relief is late, the officer on board is asked to extend. One extension becomes two, fatigue builds up, and the risk of a mistake grows exactly when the vessel is engaged in demanding operations. The Maritime Labour Convention limits how long a seafarer can serve on board before repatriation, so extensions are not an open-ended solution. Seafarers who are repeatedly extended also tend not to come back, which shrinks the pool even further. Late changes are expensive in logistics too. Last-minute flights, hotel stays, launch boats and helicopter seats cost far more than a change planned weeks ahead. And every rushed decision raises the chance of sending someone who does not fully meet the client's requirements, which can trigger a fresh round of audits and, in the worst case, a request to replace the person who has just joined. Practice 1: Plan rotations as a pipeline, not a vacancy The most effective operators stop thinking about vacancies and start thinking about pipelines. For every DP-critical position on every vessel, they know who is on board now, who relieves him next, and who is the backup if the relief falls through. That means keeping the relief identified at least one contract ahead, with certificate expiry dates, DP hours, medicals, visas and client-specific training on file. It means tracking when each officer's DP certificate needs revalidation and making sure his next assignment keeps the sea time flowing. And it means agreeing rotation patterns with seafarers early, so that they plan their lives around the schedule instead of taking another job when the call finally comes. Practice 2: Build a verified talent pool, not a shortlist Traditional recruitment often runs through a chain: the operator asks a manning agent, who asks a sub-agent, who calls his contacts. By the time a shortlist arrives, days have passed and nobody has a clear view of the wider market. Each link in the chain adds cost and removes transparency. That model is changing, and we see it every day on our own platform. More DP officers, engineers and ratings now look for a job at sea directly online, posting their CVs, certificates and sea-service records where shipowners can see them. For operators, this opens access to candidates who are not tied to a single agency and who can be contacted the same day. Direct access only works if the information is reliable. Operators should verify certificates against the issuing administrations, check references from previous masters and companies, and confirm DP logbooks before an offer is made. Over time, the candidates who pass these checks form a verified pool that can be called upon whenever a position opens, instead of starting from zero each time. JobMarineMan: shipowners search a database of 200,000 seafarer profiles and post vacancies directly Marine MAN / jobmarineman.com Practice 3: Measure crew management like any other operational function Fuel consumption, downtime and maintenance backlogs are measured on every well-run vessel. Crewing deserves the same discipline. Treating crew management as an operational function means agreeing on a small set of indicators and reviewing them as seriously as technical performance. Useful indicators include time to fill a vacancy by rank, the share of crew changes made on schedule, the number of contract extensions, retention rate by rank and vessel, and the proportion of candidates who pass client vetting at the first attempt. None of these are complicated to track, yet many companies only discover a crewing problem when a vessel is already short-handed. If crew management is outsourced, the same indicators belong in the service agreement. A provider who reports against them every month gives the operator early warning and a basis for improvement. A provider who only sends invoices does not. Practice 4: Keep the people you already have The fastest way to fill a position is never to lose the person in it. Offshore seafarers have options, and they choose employers who respect their time. Reliable rotations matter more than almost anything else. A seafarer who knows exactly when he will go home, and whose relief turns up on the agreed date, has little reason to look elsewhere. Wages paid on time and in full, clear contract terms and decent conditions on board come next. Career progression is the third factor. Junior DPOs want a path to senior DPO and then to master; engineers want exposure to modern power and propulsion systems. Operators that plan promotions and training, rather than leaving them to chance, keep their best people and build the next generation of DP-qualified officers from within. Every officer promoted internally is one less vacancy to fill from an overheated market. Practice 5: Grow your own DP officers The BIMCO/ICS Seafarer Workforce Report has been warning for years about a shortage of officers, and the offshore sector is named among those where management-level deck officers are hardest to find. Every conference discusses it. Very few companies do anything structural about it. We decided not to wait. JobMarineMan is the first and, as far as I know, still the only crewing platform in the world with a working mentorship programme for seafarers. It is not a plan or a pilot; it is live today. Experienced masters, chief engineers and DP officers apply to become mentors, Marine MAN verifies their sea service and approves them, and from that moment they are visible to every seafarer on the platform. A junior officer picks the mentor whose career looks like the one he wants and contacts him directly; the mentor sets his own terms and agrees them with the seafarer, and we stay out of that conversation. Our job is to make sure every mentor is real, qualified and worth listening to. For an offshore operator, this is a pipeline of the next generation of DP-qualified officers being built today, not a hope that the market will somehow produce them. Mentorship on JobMarineMan: experienced officers and engineers guide the next generation of specialist seafarers Marine MAN / jobmarineman.com Practice 6: Make the first week count Even the best candidate needs time to become effective on a new vessel. Offshore units differ widely in DP systems, deck equipment and company procedures, and the first days on board decide how quickly a new officer settles in. A structured familiarisation programme, a proper handover from the outgoing officer and a clear contact person ashore reduce the risk of errors and make it more likely that the newcomer will return for the next contract. What to ask a crew management partner Many operators outsource part or all of their crewing. The right partner saves time and money; the wrong one simply moves the problem from the operator's desk to a supplier's inbox. A few questions help to tell the difference: • How many DP-qualified officers and offshore-experienced ratings can you present for our vessel types, and how quickly? • How do you verify certificates, DP logbooks and references, and can we see the evidence? • Which countries do you source from, and how do you handle visas and travel for each of them? • How do you handle wages, social obligations and compliance with the Maritime Labour Convention? • Which indicators will you report, and how often? • What happens when a candidate fails client vetting or leaves the vessel early? These are the questions I would ask if I were on the operator's side of the table. Clear answers to them say more about a provider than any brochure. How we work at Marine MAN Marine MAN has worked with shipowners and managers on these questions since 2007. We are an IMO DOC holder and have been certified to ISO 9001:2015 by Bureau Veritas for crew manning and management services since 2017. At any given time, around 750 seafarers serve on board client vessels through Marine MAN, and we source crews from Ukraine, Georgia, India, Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Vietnam and the Philippines. Our platform JobMarineMan, a seaman jobsite available in 11 languages, holds 200,000 seafarer CVs. It connects shipowners and operators with candidates directly, without a chain of intermediaries, while our team takes over verification, documentation and mobilisation when needed. In my experience, offshore operators rarely lack candidates on paper. What they lack is time to find the right ones and confidence that the documents are real. Our job is to give them both: direct access to people and a process that checks every certificate before anyone boards. Conclusion The offshore fleet cannot grow faster than the crews who run it. DP-qualified officers, experienced anchor-handling crews and engineers who understand modern power systems will remain in demand for years. Operators that plan rotations as pipelines, build verified talent pools, measure crewing performance, grow their own officers through mentorship, onboard new people properly and look after the crews they already have will lose fewer days to late crew changes and find the right people before the gap appears, not after. About the author In 2007, a 20-year-old deck officer from Kherson looked at how seafarers found work and decided it was broken. Contracts came by fax. Agencies sat between a captain and his next ship like toll booths, each one taking a cut and adding a week. Pavel Manchenko had been on the other side of that chain, on the bridge, waiting for a call that never came on time. So he founded Marine MAN to fix it. Nineteen years later, he is still not 40, and the fix has become an ecosystem: recruitment offices in Ukraine, Georgia, India, Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Vietnam and the Philippines under one Marine MAN umbrella, connected on a single platform where AI now makes the first contact with a candidate and a human makes the decision. The numbers behind it: 200,000 seafarer profiles in the database, around 750 seafarers on board client vessels at any moment, and more than 35,000 seafarers who found their job through the platform. He holds a Master's degree from the Kyiv State Academy of Water Transport and is a certified DPA, CSO and MLC 2006 auditor, and he uses all of it: he still consults and mentors shipowners and crews on compliance, and he looks at every crew list the way an inspector would, because he has stood on the deck those inspectors walk. Then came February 2022. Marine MAN's head office and most of its core staff were in Kherson, the first regional capital in Ukraine to be occupied. Of all the crewing companies in the country, Pavel's was the first to find out what war actually means: colleagues behind the front line, phones that stopped answering, a company that had to be rebuilt piece by piece from wherever people managed to get out. Through all of it, the vessels stayed crewed and the seafarers got paid. That is not a line in a brochure; it is what Pavel's team actually did in 2022. Ask him how, and the answer is short: "Never retreat, never surrender, and keep faith in God." He has the energy of a founder half his age and the experience of one twice it. If you want to talk about how your fleet is crewed, talk to Pavel. Let's discuss cooperation. Want to know how our team can help your business? articles.title: KONGSBERG Launches Two New Sonars, Expands AI Partnership with Viam

articles.body: KONGSBERG Launches Two New Sonars, Expands AI Partnership with Viam Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 3, 2026 (Credit: KONGSBERG) KONGSBERG has launched two new underwater surveillance sonars for maritime security and critical infrastructure protection, while expanding its collaboration with Viam to develop an AI-powered virtual sonar operator. The new Aegir17 and Aegir57N systems expand the company's Aegir SSA (Subsea Situational Awareness) family to three models, KONGSBERG said. The Aegir17 is a long-range, 360-degree sonar designed for larger maritime platforms, using a lower acoustic frequency and larger transducer to provide greater detection range and definition than the existing Aegir57. The Aegir57N is a compact matrix sonar designed for navigation and security applications, directing acoustic beams towards selected areas to provide detailed information about the water column and seabed. The system supports forward-looking navigation in poorly charted waters and obstacle detection, while its compact design and Ethernet interface allow integration with unmanned surface vessels, fixed installations and other platforms. The two models complement the Aegir57, introduced in August 2026, which provides 360-degree subsea monitoring with detection ranges of up to 2,000 metres. Alongside the hardware expansion, KONGSBERG is strengthening its collaboration with US-based automation platform Viam to develop an AI-powered virtual sonar operator capable of automatically detecting and tracking underwater objects. The technology is intended particularly for uncrewed vessels and fixed monitoring installations, reducing the need for continuous human monitoring and allowing operators to oversee multiple remote installations. "Fish-finding and infrastructure protection are very different applications, but the challenge is similar: turning the constant flow of data that sonar generates into clear, actionable information about what's happening underwater," said Eliot Horowitz, Founder and CEO of Viam. The project builds on the companies' existing Sonar AI system developed for Simrad sonars, which automatically detects fish and alerts crews in real time. KONGSBERG said customers will be able to use existing trained AI models or implement their own models for specific environments and surveillance requirements. The first commercial delivery of an Aegir sonar is scheduled for November 2026. KONGSBERG is also integrating its subsea surveillance capabilities with satellite-based monitoring, coastal radar, drone detection and passive acoustic systems, while its HUGIN autonomous underwater vehicles provide additional underwater inspection and investigation capabilities.

articles.title: Port of Hueneme advances container export plans amid auto cargo decline
articles.summary: The Port of Hueneme is developing a new container export initiative targeting agricultural shipments from California to Asian markets, as the port seeks to diversify cargo activity following a decline in automobile volumes. The initiative was outlined during the port’s 2026 State of the Port presentation, held in...
articles.body: The Port of Hueneme is developing a new container export initiative targeting agricultural shipments from California to Asian markets, as the port seeks to diversify cargo activity following a decline in automobile volumes. The initiative was outlined during the port’s 2026 State of the Port presentation, held in late October and detailed in an announcement issued on 2 November. According to the port, automobile volumes fell by 13% during the latest fiscal year, with tariffs contributing to the decline. However, higher high-and-heavy cargo volumes and a slight increase in container imports helped support its overall financial performance. The proposed export initiative aims to use available container capacity to transport agricultural products from Ventura County to Asian markets. The port has not disclosed a launch date, expected shipment volumes or specific shipping partners. The development reflects the port’s efforts to expand its cargo base beyond established automobile and refrigerated produce operations. Infrastructure investment and cargo diversification The Port of Hueneme also reported approximately US$246 million in active grant-funded infrastructure projects. These investments are directed towards improving cargo-handling capacity, operational efficiency and environmental performance. The figure represents the value of ongoing projects rather than newly announced funding. Meanwhile, the port reported 70% growth over the past decade, while operating revenue increased by 77% between 2015 and 2026. The port remains the largest banana-handling port in the United States, the leading blueberry port on the US West Coast and the country’s fourth-largest automobile port, according to figures presented by its management. Chief Executive Officer and Port Director Kristin Decas highlighted the port’s operational development and its contribution to the regional economy. The port currently accounts for nearly 5% of Ventura County’s gross domestic product. Alongside its commercial expansion, the port continues to pursue its target of achieving zero-emission operations by 2030. Its recently energised solar canopy is expected to generate enough electricity annually to power the equivalent of approximately 250 homes. The port also reported that infrastructure projects carried out under its Project Labor Agreement have created 896 jobs to date. Looking ahead, the Port of Hueneme plans to continue upgrading its facilities while developing new cargo opportunities and strengthening its position in international trade.

ELPI has also secured a long-term marine services contract worth Rp2.39trn ($131.69m) for the planned floating LNG development in Bintuni Bay, West Papua. articles.title: Stillstrom Builds Vessel-Mounted System for Direct Offshore Wind Charging
articles.summary: Stillstrom by Maersk has completed the construction and factory acceptance testing of what it describes as the world's first 11 kV vessel-mounted connection unit designed to charge service operation vessels (SOVs) directly from offshore wind farms.The milestone…
articles.body: Stillstrom Builds Vessel-Mounted System for Direct Offshore Wind Charging Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 3, 2026 (Credit: Stillstrom by Maersk) Stillstrom by Maersk has completed the construction and factory acceptance testing of what it describes as the world's first 11 kV vessel-mounted connection unit designed to charge service operation vessels (SOVs) directly from offshore wind farms. The milestone, witnessed by DNV, marks the completion of testing for Stillstrom's Vessel Container Unit (VCU), a modular system designed to transfer electricity from offshore wind infrastructure to vessel batteries. The containerised unit houses an 11 kV connector package and can be installed at the bow, stern or beneath the deck of a vessel, allowing integration into both newbuilds and existing vessels. The unit can also be transferred between vessels where onboard cabling permits, while its integrated funnel enables charging at an optimal vessel heading, with the dynamic positioning operator retaining control over charging and disconnection. The system incorporates control technology and safety interlocks designed to support repeated offshore connections and disconnections. “High-voltage power has never been transferred to a vessel offshore in this way, and the connector package inside our VCU represents several years of careful development and testing,” said Graeme Wood, Stillstrom UK Managing Director. (Credit: Stillstrom by Maersk) Work on the wind farm topsides interface is continuing, with the complete charging system expected to be ready for extended offshore trials by summer 2027. Stillstrom is also developing a second-generation version of the VCU, known as Mark 2, which aims to move from the current semi-automatic alignment system towards full automation. The company’s offshore charging technology is designed to supply renewable electricity to fully electric and hybrid service operation vessels, using systems integrated into offshore wind farm structures or standalone offshore installations.

articles.title: Wärtsilä Helps Chevron Cut Methane Emissions with LNG Carriers Upgrade
articles.summary: Wärtsilä has completed the conversion of one engine on each of three LNG carriers operated by Chevron Transport Corporation from dual-fuel to spark gas operation, as part of a project aimed at reducing methane emissions from the vessels.The…
articles.body: Wärtsilä Helps Chevron Cut Methane Emissions with LNG Carriers Upgrade Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 3, 2026 (Credit: Chevron Shipping) Wärtsilä has completed the conversion of one engine on each of three LNG carriers operated by Chevron Transport Corporation from dual-fuel to spark gas operation, as part of a project aimed at reducing methane emissions from the vessels. The conversions involve modifying Wärtsilä 50DF engines to use spark ignition instead of diesel pilot fuel to initiate combustion, allowing for a more optimized combustion process and reduced methane slip. Methane slip refers to uncombusted methane that escapes into the atmosphere from LNG fuel. Three additional vessel conversions are planned for later in 2026 and during 2027, bringing the total number of vessels covered by the project to six, according to Wärtsilä. The conversion technology uses an electrically controlled pre-combustion chamber valve, with Wärtsilä estimating that it can reduce methane emissions to 1.1% of fuel use on an IMO-weighted E2-cycle average. “Advancing lower-emission shipping will require both technology innovation and industry collaboration. Through projects like this, we can gain valuable operational insights, evaluate solutions and contribute to the collective experience needed to help move the industry forward while continuing to provide safe and reliable transport of energy,” said Barbara Pickering, President of Chevron Shipping. Wärtsilä noted the spark gas conversion technology is also available for other vessels equipped with its existing 50DF engines for diesel-electric propulsion, the majority of which are LNG carriers.

articles.title: Rossi EP Winch: a new approach to winch gearbox design
articles.summary: Developed for marine, construction and mining applications, EP Winch combines a rotating housing, advanced simulations and experimental...
articles.body: Branded Content November 3, 2026 · 1 minute ago Rossi EP Winch: a new approach to winch gearbox design Written in partnership with Rossi 7 minutes read LinkedIn X Email EP Winch a Bauma @Rossi Developed for marine, construction and mining applications, EP Winch combines a rotating housing, advanced simulations and experimental validation in a compact and reliable solution. The gearbox will be exhibited at Offshore Energy Exhibition & Conference, where Rossi Benelux will meet companies and professionals from the marine and offshore sectors on 24 and 25 November in Amsterdam at stand 1.225. Compactness, load capacity, reliability, and ease of integration are currently some of the main requirements in the design of gearboxes intended for winches in strategic sectors. In addition to these requirements, there is a need to ensure reliability in the most demanding work cycles, ease of assembly, and the ability to adapt the product to the characteristics of the specific application. From these premises comes EP Winch, the new planetary gearbox with a rotating housing developed by Rossi for winches. The product expands a range that has represented one of the company's distinctive competencies for decades and introduces a solution designed to meet complex application needs through compactness, robustness, and customization possibilities. " With EP Winch, we didn't just want to add a new product to our range, " explains Davide Ferrari , R&D Manager for Planetary Gearboxes and Deputy CTO at Rossi. " The goal was to put our know-how at the service of the customer, developing a solution capable of better integrating into their applications and evolving along with their needs. " A rotating housing to integrate the gearbox into the drum The distinctive feature of EP Winch is the rotating housing configuration, which allows the gearbox to be incorporated directly into the winch drum. This solution helps contain dimensions and addresses one of the most frequent constraints in marine, mining, and construction applications, where space availability can influence the design of the entire machine. Hoisting for winder machin - mining @Rossi Integrating the gearbox into the drum offers manufacturers greater design freedom and allows for optimized configurations without sacrificing the load capacity and robustness required in heavy-duty applications. The design therefore involved every component of the transmission, with the goal of fully exploiting the structural capabilities of the system while maintaining the safety margins required by lifting and handling systems. The gear configurations ensure high load capacity, strength, and a reduction in noise and vibration during operation. FEM and CFD to verify structure, lubrication, and heat exchange Alongside FEM structural analyses, used to verify the behavior of components under load, Rossi used CFD (Computational Fluid Dynamics) simulations dedicated to studying internal lubricant flows. The analyses allowed for the optimization of the gearbox geometries and the verification of correct oil distribution under different operating conditions. One of the most delicate aspects, in fact, concerns operation at high speeds, which is required especially during no-load rope recovery, when the winch must complete the movement in the shortest possible time. As the rotation speed increases, lubricant management becomes more complex: it is necessary to ensure that the oil correctly reaches the moving parts and, at the same time, limit the temperature increase during operation. Through simulations, it was possible to study how much oil could circulate inside the gearbox, verify the input of fresh lubricant, and facilitate the recovery of the heated oil. The analyses therefore allowed for the identification of configurations capable of ensuring adequate lubrication even at the highest speeds expected during use. The joint work on structure, fluid dynamics, and thermal behavior contributed to defining the gearbox's operating limits with greater precision and to improving the product's efficiency, durability, and reliability. Testing torque and rope pull together After numerical simulations, EP Winch was subjected to an experimental validation program in Rossi's test rooms. A prototype with characteristics similar to those of the production gearbox was built, and test benches capable of reproducing the stresses typical of the application were prepared. During the tests, the gearbox was operated by simultaneously applying the transmitted torque and the radial load that simulates the pull exerted by the rope on the winch. This configuration allowed for the evaluation of the product's behavior in conditions close to real ones and for the verification of multiple parameters within the same test runs. The tests confirmed the robustness of the solutions adopted and provided the data necessary for dialogue with DNV, an international certification body particularly relevant to the marine sector. To obtain the DNV Type Approval Certificate, Rossi did not limit itself to an internal verification conducted based on international standards, but applied specific tests and criteria required by the certifying body. The certification thus strengthens the suitability of EP Winch for applications where documented compliance and reliability are essential requirements. The work carried out during validation also contributed to the definition of an analysis methodology related to planetary gearboxes, which will be presented as part of an important international technical update promoted by AGMA to be held in Chicago in October 2026. An installation designed to reduce time and risks Ease of installation was considered from the very first design phases. The connections to the main motors available on the market were developed to allow for motor coupling without having to disassemble structural elements of the gearbox, as can happen with other configurations. The advantage for the customer is not just about reducing assembly times. Avoiding the disassembly of flanges or internal components limits the risk of oil leaks, contamination, and incorrect assembly, making all operations simpler and safer even when performed by non-specialized personnel. The adopted configuration therefore facilitates both the initial mounting on the winch and subsequent maintenance activities, helping to reduce operational complexity and downtime. Tower crane hoisting winch - construction @Rossi From product range to application solution EP Winch fits into Rossi's ability to start from a broad catalog and consolidated expertise in transmissions to identify the most effective configuration in relation to the application and requirements. The evaluation does not concern only the individual gearbox; operating conditions, duty cycles, durability requirements, motorization, dimensions, and integration methods are analyzed as parts of a single system. This expertise also allows for combining different gearboxes and technologies when the most effective configuration requires a non-standard solution. “ Partnerships with customers represent a fundamental part of our way of working, ” emphasizes Stefano Cioffi , Head of Segments Marine and Construction. “ Engaging with them from the early stages allows us to develop products based on real application needs and to transform every project into an opportunity for mutual improvement. ” Dialogue with the market also accompanied the initial development of EP Winch. The gearbox was, in fact, used by some Spanish charter customers in the marine sector, who were involved in a pilot project launched in 2025. Field applications allowed for the collection of concrete feedback and the verification of the product within real operating conditions. Charter customer @Rossi The first projects following the launch also confirm the possibility of using EP Winch not only for new applications but also for rethinking existing systems. In one case, the new gearbox was proposed to a customer who was using a previous configuration and had the need to reduce the costs of the installed solution. Starting from the system's operating conditions, Rossi replaced the previous configuration with a customized solution based on EP Winch, maintaining focus on the required performance and improving the overall economic sustainability of the project. Dialogue with the marine and offshore market at Offshore Energy Exhibition & Conference This dialogue with the market will continue at Offshore Energy Exhibition & Conference on 24 and 25 November 2026 in Amsterdam, where the Rossi Benelux team will meet companies and professionals from the marine and offshore sectors at stand 1.225, and EP Winch will be on display. “ Offshore Energy is an important opportunity for Rossi Benelux to engage with manufacturers and operators in the sector. Bringing EP Winch to the exhibition allows us to demonstrate the solution in practice and, above all, to understand the specific requirements of different projects, ” adds Jorian Bos , Branch Manager of Rossi Benelux. The event will provide an opportunity to explore how Rossi’s engineering expertise can meet the needs of the most demanding winch applications. “ Every marine and offshore application has specific requirements. Staying close to our customers allows us to understand these challenges and identify the most suitable solution for each project, ” explains Alexander van Bendegem , Area Sales Manager & Key Account Manager of Rossi Benelux. Trawler winch - marine @Rossi A new piece in the Rossi planetary range EP Winch will be produced in Rossi's Lecce plants, using components sourced from the Italian and European markets. With the new rotating housing gearbox, the company expands its offering for winches and consolidates an expertise that combines mechanical design, numerical simulation, testing, and customization capabilities. The result is a product conceived to reduce dimensions, withstand heavy operating conditions, simplify installation, and adapt to the needs of manufacturers. A gearbox that stems from concrete application requirements and that, for this very reason, can become the basis for different solutions, developed together with the customer. articles.summary: What Factors Go Into a Shadow Fleet Boarding Decision Six times since September 2025, French Navy boarding teams have gone aboard a suspected shadow fleet tanker. articles.body: Shadow Fleet Interdiction Starts With Flag Verification in International Shipping News 03/11/2026 What Factors Go Into a Shadow Fleet Boarding Decision Six times since September 2025, French Navy boarding teams have gone aboard a suspected shadow fleet tanker. The latest came on October 12, 2026, when the Marine Nationale boarded DF PEAK more than 450 nautical miles south of Réunion on suspicion of sailing under a false flag. In June, DELIVER was boarded off Sicily, France’s fifth such operation. Naval planners often talk about preparing for high-intensity warfare, meaning a large-scale conflict between major military powers. The shadow fleet shows that pressure at sea is already rising well before that point. French warships are repeatedly stopping and boarding commercial tankers. Moscow calls these operations piracy. Paris says they enforce the international law of the sea. The helicopter and the boarding team are what the public sees. The work that decides whether a boarding happens, and whether it holds up afterward, starts much earlier with one question. Is this ship really who it says it is? Flag Doubts Ran Through Every French Boarding Shadow fleet tankers hide both where they are and who they are. They switch off AIS, sometimes for days at a time, and they disguise their identity through flag-hopping, invalid registrations, and repeated name changes. That identity problem is the reason most French boardings started with a doubt about the flag rather than the cargo. The pattern runs through every case.fmonths, and six jurisdictions had sanctioned it. The legal reason is straightforward. French authorities have described these operations as carried out under UNCLOS, and for DF PEAK the French Armed Forces General Staff cited Article 110, which gives warships a right of visit on the high seas when a ship is suspected of being stateless or fraudulently flagged. In other words, the flag is what gave France its legal basis. French authorities boarded DF PEAK because they suspected its flag was false, which is one of the situations Article 110 covers. That makes identity the first thing to test and the last thing a boarding team should be guessing about. By the time the helicopter is airborne, the command has already decided which ship, whether its flag is likely invalid, and whether the evidence will survive the legal challenge that follows. The Kremlin called the TAGOR seizure illegal and an act of piracy, and French prosecutors took BORACAY‘s captain and first officer into custody. A Position Report Cannot Prove a Flag Is Real AIS was built for collision avoidance, not identity assurance. The flag, name, and destination a tanker broadcasts are entered on board, and nothing in the signal checks them against a registry. The gap is wide. Windward’s Q2 2026 Maritime Risk Report counted 275 internationally trading tankers broadcasting the flag of a fraudulent registry and identified 22 fraudulent registries in use, including new false claims to Syria and Myanmar, neither of which operates an international registry. By the end of September, the IMO’s list of falsely flagged ships had reached 613, up 39% since January. Position data is no safer. The Q2 report found that GPS spoofing had generated 3.35 million false ship-to-ship meetings worldwide since late February 2026, with vessels appearing to rendezvous when no meeting took place. Proving a flag is false means checking the broadcast against evidence the ship does not control, such as registry records, IMO data, ownership chains, and the vessel’s past names and flags. Windward’s Q2 assessment found that the boardings that best withstood legal scrutiny were backed by verified flag-state data that contradicted what the vessel was broadcasting. A false flag tanker gives itself away in the records, not in its position report. Behavioral History Tells Navies Which Tanker Deserves the Helicopter There are far more candidate tankers than boarding teams. One in three Aframax and LR2 tankers worldwide is now in Windward’s tracked dark fleet, and 78% of that fleet is sanctioned by the U.S., UK, or EU, according to Windward’s Q3 2026 report. Windward’s MIOC estimated that the six European boardings in the first three months of 2026 amounted to an interception rate below 2%. Every sortie spent on the wrong ship is one not spent on the right one. Behavioral history is how that list gets ranked. A tanker’s record of flag changes, name changes, dark periods, and ownership links says far more about the likelihood of a false flag than any single position report. DEYNA shows what that record can look like. In an analysis published after the French boarding, Windward’s MIOC traced the tanker’s voyage from Murmansk. It entered Russian waters on February 22, 2026, went dark for about 48 hours, and reappeared with a new MMSI number under the Mozambican flag. After a second dark period of similar length, its draft had risen from 8 to 14 meters, a sign it had loaded. Since 2020, the vessel had changed identity 13 times, including 8 flag changes in 13 months, and six jurisdictions had sanctioned it. None of those indicators alone proves a false flag. Read together and checked against registry data, they move a tanker to the top of the list long before anyone decides to board it. Allied Navies Need the Same Picture Before the Boarding None of these operations was purely national. USNI News reported that earlier French seizures in the Mediterranean were supported by fast patrol boats of the Royal Navy’s Gibraltar Squadron, which shadowed the suspect tankers and reported their movements. French military officials said that the UK gathered and shared the intelligence that enabled the GRINCH interception. DELIVER was stopped with help from the Royal Navy and EUNAVFOR MED. The political framework is coalition-based as well. In January 2026, fourteen European states issued a joint letter warning shadow fleet vessels that they could be boarded and seized under UNCLOS provisions on stateless ships. The target set is also shifting. Russia moved 84 dark fleet tankers onto its own registry in Q3 2026 and is now the largest flag in the dark fleet. Each tanker that reflags to Russia leaves the pool of suspected false flags, and the vessels that remain get harder to find and to prove. Allies who shadow, report, and board together need to work from the same identity picture, with the same history behind each vessel, before anyone commits a boarding team. A disagreement about a flag discovered on deck comes too late. Identity Intelligence Is the Layer Under Every Boarding Each boarding in this campaign is the visible end of a quieter task. Someone decided which ship, tested its flag against the records, weighed its history, and shared that picture with the allies standing by. All-source intelligence is built for that task. It fuses AIS with satellite imagery, RF detection, registry and ownership data, sanctions lists, years of behavioral history, and any other source the mission calls for, then tests what a vessel claims against what it has actually done. The result is a ranked, evidence-backed view of which shadow fleet tankers are most likely sailing under a flag they have no right to fly. Windward will be at Euronaval in Paris, November 3 to 6, in Hall 6 at booth J128. To go deeper, explore Windward’s shadow fleet coverage or book a meeting. articles.body: LNG Bunker Snapshot: Singapore-ARA spread narrows as European gas supply concerns lift Rotterdam in International Shipping News 03/11/2026 Weekly changes in LNG bunker prices: ARA up by $97/mt to $1,873/mt Singapore up by $74/mt to $1,939/mt Baltics up by $97/mt to $1,976/mt ARA Rotterdam’s LNG bunker price rose for the fifth consecutive week, climbing by $97/mt week-on-week to $1,873/mt. The rise tracked an approximately 3% increase in the front-month Dutch TTF Natural Gas contract over the week. TTF is Europe’s benchmark gas price. A higher LNG bunker premium also supported the price, rising by $0.73/MMBtu to $3.17/MMBtu ($165/mt). TTF rose amid expectations of increased gas-fired power generation, following a decline in wind power generation and unplanned outages at Norwegian gas production facilities, according to the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security (JOGMEC). “The market has moved higher, with little sign of imminent relief in Persian Gulf LNG flows,” said ING Bank head of commodities strategy Warren Patterson. He added that several unplanned outages in Norway would add to supply concerns. TTF found support from continued LNG supply disruption via Hormuz, colder temperatures, four unplanned outages in Norway at Kollsnes and Kårstø, and some countries starting to withdraw gas from storage, International Energy Agency (IEA) gas analyst Greg Molnár said. TTF was also driven by forecasts of falling temperatures across Europe, concerns over gas supplies next winter, and supply uncertainties arising from the shutdown of all trains at Freeport LNG in the US and shipping disruptions in the Middle East, JOGMEC added. EU-wide underground gas storage stood at 74.7% on 30 October, almost unchanged from the previous weekend but 10.5% below the level recorded during the same period last year, according to Gas Infrastructure Europe. “EU storage levels are at their lowest since 2013,” Molnár said. Weather forecasts also turned colder and calmer over the weekend, adding bullish support to a market already under pressure from Middle East uncertainty and low gas storage, Mind Energy said. Rotterdam’s liquefied biomethane (LBM) price rose by $100/mt week-on-week to $2,575/mt. Biomethane prices in Germany have risen on the back of higher gas prices rather than a bigger green premium, said Henning Dicks, co-founder of agriportance. “This is a gas rally, not a green gas boom in Germany,” according to Dicks, with the increase a windfall from the gas market driven by the Middle East crisis and low storage levels. Singapore Singapore’s LNG bunker price rose by $74/mt week-on-week to $1,939/mt, a smaller increase than Rotterdam’s. This narrowed Singapore’s premium over ARA to $66/mt from $89/mt a week earlier. Singapore’s LNG bunker price typically tracks the front-month NYMEX Japan/Korea Marker (JKM), which has risen by $1.42/MMBtu ($74/mt) to $32.84/MMBtu ($1,708/mt). The bunker premium over JKM was unchanged at $4.45/MMBtu ($231/mt). JKM rose on the back of rising European gas prices amid falling temperatures and low underground gas storage levels in Europe, according to JOGMEC. “European benchmark prices have gained more than 200% since the start of the Middle East conflict, but high prices are failing to deter Asian buyers,” said ANZ Bank senior commodity strategist Daniel Hynes. LNG shipments through Hormuz are still just 30% of pre-war levels, with the disruption to cargoes that made up almost a fifth of global exports last year sending Asian prices to their highest levels since 2022, said Bloomberg News Energy Asia team leader Stephen Stapczynski. In other LNG bunker news, Norwegian shipping company Wallenius Wilhelmsen has signed agreements with China’s Jinling Shipyard for four pure car and truck carriers (PCTCs). Japanese shipping company Mitsui O.S.K. Lines (MOL) has taken delivery of an LNG-capable dual-fuel coal carrier fitted with a wind sail. Norwegian shipping company Utkilen has taken delivery of M/T Listraum, the second of four LNG-capable tankers being built at Icdas Shipyard in Türkiye. Japanese bunker supplier Keys Bunkering West Japan (KEYS) has completed the 100th LNG delivery by its bunkering vessel Keys Azalea, supplying NYK Line’s bulk carrier SG Dawn. articles.body: Offshore operators should not wait for EU ETS clarity to act on emissions data in International Shipping News 03/11/2026 EU MRV has applied to offshore vessels of 400 GT and above since 1 January 2025, and vessels of 5,000 GT and above are scheduled to enter the EU ETS from the 2027 reporting period. On 17 July 2026, the European Commission published proposals that would revise the MRV framework from 1 January 2029 and bring offshore vessels between 400 and 5,000 GT into the ETS from 2031. These are not final, however, and must still pass through the legislative process. The question is how the rules will work offshore in practice. The International Marine Contractors Association (IMCA) has welcomed the recognition of offshore-specific terminology and operational realities, but says more clarity is needed on ports of call, cross-border operations and how the EU and UK ETS interact. I understand why that uncertainty makes operators hesitate. Waiting still costs time, though. It leaves less opportunity to establish reliable data, embed routines and show measurable improvement before regulatory or customer expectations move. Timelines also keep shifting. In August, Norway’s Ministry of Climate and Environment confirmed that FuelEU Maritime and ReFuelEU Aviation, previously expected to take effect later this year, will not enter into force for Norway before 1 January 2028. That is exactly why I would build operational and data discipline now rather than work towards a fixed date. Norway shows the direction, though. From 2029, companies operating on the Norwegian continental shelf must reduce the greenhouse gas intensity of ships used in oil and gas activity, starting at 10% for 2029-2031 and rising in stages to 40% for 2038-2040. Rystad Energy estimates close to 300 offshore vessels fall within scope, and that most of them, including LNG dual-fuel units, would miss the first threshold based on how they operate today. Regional rules tend to come first in maritime, with global frameworks following. Similar expectations are building outside Europe, with ADNOC’s net-zero programme increasingly shaping how fleet performance is measured across its logistics operations. Fleet renewal will not address this challenge any time soon. Newbuild and retrofit programmes are moving slowly, so the lever most operators have today is running the existing fleet more efficiently. The need to measure performance does not go away with new engines or fuels either, it simply moves onto different equipment. Damien Bertin, Business Director, Opsealog The business case also doesn’t depend on regulation. Fuel is the most immediate cost, but a single daily fuel figure does not tell you where it was used. OSVs move between transit, dynamic positioning, standby and port activity at very different engine loads, so consumption needs measuring by operating mode rather than averaging across the fleet. Our work with Tullow Ghana’s MV Flat Confidence, a Ghanaian-owned AHTS, shows the scale. The performance programme recorded a fuel reduction of 732.6 m³ and avoided 1,984 tonnes of CO₂. ADNOC Logistics & Services’ fleetwide programme, which now covers more than 100 OSVs, reports savings above 20,400 m³ of fuel and 55,600 tonnes of CO₂. A separate programme with a West African operator recorded a further 1,108 m³ saved. In practice, being a front-runner means structured fuel and emissions monitoring, a few operational KPIs owned by named people and each tied to a decision, and a loop that validates the data, finds where performance departs from standard, acts, and checks the improvement lasts. Common reporting standards have been discussed for years without adoption. Energy LEAP has published a draft Vessel Emissions Reporting Standard for consultation, and ISOA worked in a similar direction earlier, but data infrastructure, owner and operator alignment, and ambitions set further ahead than fleets could deliver held both back. Operators who build reporting discipline now can help shape those standards, rather than inherit them. The sector remains cautious, and this was reflected in industry discussions earlier this year, where participants rated its digital maturity two out of five, even as efficiency came up again and again as a priority. Charterers and energy companies are also showing more interest in structured emissions reporting, including Scope 3, and credible fuel and emissions data may increasingly support contract discussions. That varies by customer and region, so it is an emerging expectation rather than a universal rule for choosing vessels. Our advice is not to wait for regulation to force the issue. Reliable data, clear operating standards, defined responsibility and a process for turning insight into action support commercial efficiency, emissions transparency and future compliance alike. At Opsealog, we see the operators who build these into everyday fleet management cutting waste now and ending up better placed for whatever regulatory obligations emerge. Source: By Damien Bertin, Business Director, Opsealog 2026-11-03 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: LNG shipping stocks: Back toward 230 points in International Shipping News 03/11/2026 The UP World LNG Shipping Index halted its slide and gained 7.92 points (3.58%) to close at 229.39, back within striking distance of the 230 mark, while the S&P 500 lost 0.57%. The only meaningful decline was Pan Ocean (−6%), pulling back into its high-level range, with Dynagas and BP each off 1.8%. The updated Crystal Ball turns more constructive: Qatar’s moves to honour its commitments have lifted market sentiment, and supplier diversification (now including a US deal for Bangladesh) is reshaping the market beyond price alone. UPI & SPX The UP World LNG Shipping Index, which tracks 21 listed LNG shipping companies, gained 7.92 points (3.58%) to close at 229.39 points, while the S&P 500 index lost 0.57%. Venture Global has commenced commercial operations at the Plaquemines terminal.
