The average price for December delivery to north-east #Asia was estimated at $32.50 per million British thermal units (mmBtu) in the week ending 30 October, the highest since mid-December 2022 and up from $30.50/mmBtu the previous week. In addition to attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis on Saudi energy and transport infrastructure, which heightened supply uncertainty, prices were also supported by buying interest from importers in Vietnam and India via spot tenders. In Europe, S&P Global Energy assessed its daily Northwest Europe LNG price benchmark for cargoes delivered in November on an ex-ship basis at $31.910/mmBtu on Thursday, a discount of $0.50/mmBtu to the price at the Dutch TTF gas hub, as colder weather, historically low gas storage levels and geopolitical uncertainty reinforced concerns over winter supply. Spot rates for LNG tankers rose, particularly in the Pacific, where they climbed to $44,500 per day, whilst in the Atlantic they rose to $28,000 per day, according to Spark Commodities. Constituents New Fortress Energy (NASDAQ: NFE) has confirmed its high volatility, rising 41 per cent last week after reports that it agreed to lease 10 mobile turbines capable of generating up to 300 MW of power to an unnamed “US-based investment-grade company”. The lease has an initial term of five years, with turbine deliveries scheduled between the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027; the deal is expected to boost the company’s revenue, but the financial terms have not been disclosed. Excelerate Energy (NYSE: EE) capitalised on support to rise more than 9 per cent, pushing the price toward resistance, which also marks the threshold for a higher level. Nakilat (QSE: QGTS) moved into third place thanks to positive news, rising by 7.6 per cent. The rise was even higher than during the week, but it failed to sustain that level. This is mainly due to uncertainty over flows through the Strait of Hormuz; however, ‘coincidentally’, it also failed to break through the resistance level around the four-riyal mark. Technically and geopolitically, the rise is positive, but it is not yet enough to change investors’ outlook. Capital Clean Energy Carriers (NASDAQ: CCEC) posted the second 7 per cent rise of last week, having also capitalised on a rebound from support. Resistance lies at around $24; until then, the trend remains sideways. All three Japanese stocks rose by around six per cent. Mitsui O.S.K. Lines (TSE: 9104) gained 6.45 per cent, NYK Line (TSE: 9101) rose by 5.88 per cent and “K” Line (TSE: 9107) climbed by 5.83 per cent. The percentage gains are therefore very similar, but the chart patterns are both similar and different. All three broke through their closing price resistance levels and closed above them, though they remain within a zone of strong resistance. The difference is that MOL is the only one already trending upward and no longer trading within a sideways range. If this momentum holds, the other two are likely to follow suit and break out of the sideways range. The most significant recent rise was recorded by COSCO Shipping Energy Transportation (SS: 600026), at 3.2 per cent. This is a case of ‘up but not really up’. The price ended the week before last at the magnetic support level of the lowest prices, and last week it attempted a more significant rise above the closing price support level. It did not succeed; the price was pushed back down, and the rise therefore only reached those closing prices. This may or may not be positive. Something similar can be said of Golar LNG (NASDAQ: GLNG), which is also trading near its support level and rose by 1.4 per cent. Here, too, the rally was pushed back. Chevron (NYSE: CVX) gained nearly one per cent, driven by positive economic outlooks. The price reached a new high. Tsakos Energy Navigation (NYSE: TEN) is trading at a key resistance level near its all-time high. Although the price fell, it rose by 0.7 per cent week-on-week. This was due to a move at the key resistance level, where the gap opening also marked a high and the price returned to its previous closing price. Two other companies remain, both showing identical growth of 0.47 per cent. These are Shell (NYSE: SHEL) and Korea Line Corporation (KRX: 005880). Shell, as Chevron mentioned above, continues to rise. KLC fended off a decline attempt and held steady at the previous closing price. It thus continues to move sideways. The largest – and, in fact, the only significant – decline was that of Pan Ocean (KRX: 028670), which, with a six per cent fall, retreated from an attempt to continue its rise back into a sideways range. At the same time, this range is at its highest price levels. The second-largest falls did not even reach two per cent. Both Dynagas LNG Partners (NYSE: DLNG) and BP (NYSE: BP) fell by 1.8 per cent. Whilst BP is in a similar pattern to Shell and Chevron, DLNG is testing this year’s lowest prices. However, it remains within the magnetic support range, albeit only just. ADNOC Logistics & Services halted its decline by returning to the upper edge of the previous sideways range, which formed at the end of July. FLEX LNG (NYSE: FLNG) has been trading at support for the third week running. While it rebounded from a fall below this level the week before last, last week saw a rejection of any upward movement. The result was a weekly decline of 0.7 per cent. MISC (KLSE: 3816) continued to trade within the spring-time sideways range, to which it had returned the week before last. The week saw both gains and losses, resulting in a flat performance of -0.6 per cent. ALNG (OSE: ALNG) traded at the upper edge of its sideways range. Here too, a larger decline was rejected, resulting in a move of -0.3 per cent. Exmar (EBR: EXM) closed at the same price as it opened, with the mid-week decline being rejected. Crystal Ball Qatar remains on the sidelines among the losers of this conflict, yet its actions over the past few days have boosted market optimism. Its efforts to honour its commitments and fulfil its orders are undoubtedly a significant boost to its customers. US producers are seeking to capitalise on the resulting vacuum by accelerating capacity expansion as supplier diversification takes place. Price is no longer the sole criterion, and even Bangladesh has announced that it has signed a long-term contract with a US producer. Whilst the coming winter months will bring increased uncertainty and a scramble for gas – partly due to the uncertain geopolitical situation, with a significant risk of further US strikes on Iran – we expect the situation to stabilise and adapt in the spring, primarily through the diversification of suppliers. articles.title: Hong Kong’s maritime future bodes well
articles.summary: The release of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region’s first five-year plan is an important moment for the city’s development. For the maritime sector, it is especially significant: It places Hong Kong’s evolution as an international maritime center within a longer-term policy framework, and gives clearer...
articles.body: Hong Kong’s maritime future bodes well in International Shipping News 03/11/2026 The release of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region’s first five-year plan is an important moment for the city’s development. For the maritime sector, it is especially significant: It places Hong Kong’s evolution as an international maritime center within a longer-term policy framework, and gives clearer direction for high-quality growth. The central government has consistently supported Hong Kong in consolidating and enhancing its status as an international maritime center. Both words matter. “Consolidating” points to Hong Kong’s established institutional foundations, international connectivity and professional services strengths. “Enhancing” means moving further up the global maritime value chain. Public discussion of Hong Kong’s maritime sector often centers on container throughput, port rankings and route networks. These indicators remain important. But if an international maritime center is understood mainly through those measures, Hong Kong’s real competitive strengths risk being understated. International shipping today is no longer simply a contest between ports. As supply chains are restructured, the green transition accelerates, geopolitical risks rise and commercial rules evolve, so competition increasingly turns to high-end services, the institutional environment and the ability to allocate global resources. The more value-added parts of the maritime industry are often not at the terminal, but in finance, insurance, ship leasing and management, legal and dispute resolution services, risk management and green transition-related services. Hong Kong’s maritime future should therefore not be framed simply as regaining a ranking or restoring a throughput level. The more important task is high-end upgrading and value creation. Hong Kong should not replicate the scale- and cost-based competition of neighboring ports, but secure a higher-value, more institutionally sophisticated and less replaceable role in the global shipping value chain. Hong Kong has the conditions to do so. Its advantage has never been merely that it has a port, but that it combines a common law system, free port status, an international financial center platform, a mature professional services market and a unique role linking the Chinese mainland with international markets. Shipping is a complex international industry built on contracts, financing, insurance, settlement, compliance and dispute resolution. Jurisdictions that provide stable, clear, credible and efficient services across these dimensions are best placed to become true modern international maritime centers. Viewed through the lens of the first five-year plan, the next step should be to deepen high value-added maritime services. The plan proposes strengthening such services, enhancing the ship registration regime, and leveraging Hong Kong’s strengths in ship management, ship finance, marine insurance and maritime arbitration. That direction comes at exactly the right time. As global shipping faces major financing needs driven by green transition, fleet renewal and changing trade patterns, Hong Kong can play a more proactive role in ship finance, leasing, green finance and related investment platforms. Marine insurance and risk management also deserve greater prominence. International shipping now faces not only traditional maritime risks, but also risks arising from war, sanctions, supply chain disruption, cybersecurity and decarbonization. Stronger capabilities in marine insurance, reinsurance, protection and indemnity, claims handling and dispute resolution would directly support Hong Kong’s international maritime center status. Maritime legal and dispute resolution services are a critical component. International shipping transactions are complex, contractual chains are long, and disputes are common. Market participants look not only at whether a port is efficient and well connected, but also at whether rules are clear, contracts can be enforced and disputes resolved reliably. Deeper integration of legal services and dispute resolution with maritime development would strengthen Hong Kong’s institutional foundations and better serve mainland enterprises going global, as well as international businesses managing cross-border activities through Hong Kong. High-end upgrading should not be seen as adding separate service lines. Hong Kong needs a high value-added maritime services ecosystem. Businesses choosing a maritime center assess whether it can connect transactions, financing, risk management and dispute resolution, and remain predictable in a complex environment. The plan’s emphasis on collaboration among industry stakeholders and training institutions, and on building a systematic training framework and stable talent pool, directly addresses the human capital needed for such an ecosystem. Hong Kong’s maritime development must also be understood within the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area and the country’s modern transport network. The plan emphasizes stronger synergy, high-quality collaborative port development, deeper cooperation with mainland and overseas shipping ports, and lower transshipment costs through a comprehensive “rail-sea-land-river” intermodal system to stabilize container throughput. As Hong Kong, Shenzhen and Guangzhou form part of the same world-class port cluster, the better path is not homogenized competition, but differentiated positioning and coordinated development. Hong Kong should retain and optimize necessary port functions. More importantly, it should focus on international connectivity, high-end services, institutional supply and global resource allocation. The plan proposes diversified and resilient international transportation corridors, faster sea-air intermodal transshipment, and stronger status as an international transshipment hub. Shenzhen and Guangzhou have advantages in hinterland, scale and manufacturing support, while Hong Kong’s strengths lie in international finance, professional services, the common law system and global networks. With clearer division of labor and stronger coordination, Hong Kong can become the high-end services hub and international functional platform for the broader Greater Bay Area port cluster. This is also part of Hong Kong’s role in serving the country’s high-standard opening-up. Building a maritime power requires not only more ports and a larger fleet, but stronger capabilities in financing, insurance, legal services, risk management and alignment with international rules. Hong Kong has a distinctive foundation in these areas, and the first five-year plan is an opportunity to align those strengths more closely with the country’s needs. Hong Kong’s next-stage maritime development should not seek to return to an earlier model based primarily on port traffic. It should respond to changing international shipping dynamics by moving toward a more value-added, higher-end and institutionally supported path. Anchored in the themes of “stabilizing container throughput, adding value, and strengthening synergy”, the first five-year plan points toward smart and green ports, logistics data interconnection, green maritime fuel, collaborative port development and high value-added maritime services. If matched by sharper policy focus, stronger cross-sector coordination and clearer functional division of labor within the Greater Bay Area, Hong Kong will be well placed to become a more influential modern hub for high-end maritime services. For the maritime sector, it is especially significant: It places Hong Kong’s evolution as an international maritime center within a longer-term policy framework, and gives clearer direction for high-quality growth.
The central government has consistently supported Hong Kong in consolidating and enhancing its status as an international maritime center.

articles.body: VesselFront receives Bureau Veritas Type approval for its VesselFront.AI Weather-Routing software in International Shipping News 03/11/2026 VesselFront, a maritime software company based in Piraeus, announces that its Vesselfront.AI software has received Type Approval from the international classification society Bureau Veritas. The approval certifies the software’s capabilities in fuel consumption calculation, emissions forecasting and support weather routing decisions. Vessels running the software can be assigned the additional class notation SMART EnE3-Em-W (rule note NR675) which .The approval is valid until March 2031 and each installation is surveyed by a Bureau Veritas representative as part of assigning the SMART EnE3-Em-W notation to the vessel. In parallel, the classification society has certified VesselFront’s quality management system in Piraeus (BV Mode II, NR320). Vesselfront.AI is a weather-routing system for commercial fleets. It accounts for the applicable regulatory framework and the operational voyage plan and, with safety of navigation as the primary criterion, determines the optimal route for each voyage. Specialised agents continuously assess weather, fuel oil consumption, compliance with environmental regulations and the vessel’s exposure to adverse sea conditions. Every recommendation is explained leg by leg, so that the master and the ship’s management can verify the reasoning behind it. “Today, the master receives a recommended route from shore with no real justification, despite bearing full responsibility for the ship and her crew. Likewise, when a speed or consumption claim arises, the charterer has to reconstruct what happened after the fact, often from incomplete data. Both need the same thing: to know why the route was chosen. The master needs it before departure, the charterer after arrival”, said Katerina Karampasi, VP Engineering at VesselFront. Every route calculated by Vesselfront.AI is subjected to binding safety constraints, including maximum significant wave height along the route, maximum and minimum sailing latitude, and no-go areas. These constraints always take precedence over fuel savings, while the system also minimises time spent in Emission Control Areas (ECAs). A patent application for Vesselfront.AI has been filed with the US Patent & Trademark Office (USPTO). The innovation of the company’s approach is also highlighted by its research contract with the European Space Agency (ESA). Source: VesselFront 2026-11-03 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: How conflicts are impacting global supply chains
articles.summary: Worries around global supply chains are back in the news: This time, it’s not an unknown virus but the conflict in the Middle East that has added to concerns about the global economy. In April, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s global supply chain pressure index rose to its highest level in four years, ...
articles.body: How conflicts are impacting global supply chains in Port News 03/11/2026 Worries around global supply chains are back in the news: This time, it’s not an unknown virus but the conflict in the Middle East that has added to concerns about the global economy. In April, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s global supply chain pressure index rose to its highest level in four years, believed to have been driven by disruption to shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz. A truce among the parties helped calm the waters in between, but it appeared to be short-lived. Hence, shipping through the strait, which had accounted for about 20% of global oil and gas exports in 2025,2 has faced renewed disruption. The impact is being felt on global supply chains through four key channels: First, diminishing supplies of crude oil from Gulf countries have potentially pushed up prices. Second, exports of natural gas, which power households and factories, have faced disruption. Refined products such as diesel and aviation fuel, too, have seen notable price increases, with the conflict in Ukraine also adding pressure. Third, global food production could face challenges as lower levels of fertilizer exports from the Gulf may affect crop yields, especially in Asia. Finally, the growing number of attacks on merchant vessels in Middle Eastern waters3 may be adding a new layer of risk and uncertainty to international trade. A crude (oil) jolt to the world According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), more than 10 million barrels per day (mbpd) of Gulf oil production remained offline in August as disruptions to maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz constrained producers’ ability to export crude oil.4 Rerouted flows through alternative pipelines and escorted tanker transits have kept some crude moving. Even so, total crude-oil exports from the Gulf were about 45% lower in August than before the conflict. Attacks on Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline in September and threats to Red Sea shipping routes may continue to place pressure on the Gulf’s oil supplies.5 Producers that are not part of the OPEC+6 group have increased output, but that may not be enough to offset the loss in crude supply. The IEA now projects global oil supply will fall by 5.7 mbpd this year. Crude inventories have likely provided some relief: The IEA estimates that 507 million barrels of global inventories have been drawn down since the conflict started, with China accounting for a large share of the most recent decline.7 Such support may, however, become less available if the conflict persists and inventories continue to dwindle. As of Sept. 18, 2026, in the United States, crude stocks in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve had fallen by 46% since the conflict began, leaving them at their lowest level since October 1982.8 The net result of this has been an increase in crude prices this year. Brent crude was trading above US$105 per barrel on Sept. 24, 2026—about 50% above its pre-conflict level and nearly 75% higher than at the end of 2025 (figure 1). Prices have been volatile, as frequent flare-ups in hostilities and intermittent negotiations keep traders on their toes. Higher prices have dampened some demand for crude oil: The IEA forecasts global oil demand could decline by 2.5 mbpd in 2026 before recovering next year. The impact on refined products and natural gas supply chains In August, exports of refined products and liquefied petroleum gas from the Gulf were nearly 60% below their February levels.9 Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries are also believed to have contributed to the problem. Russia has been a major producer of refined oil products and second only to the United States and China.10 But, with damage to its refineries, diesel output in Russia was 30% lower than in 2025, while gasoline production was down 20%. The IEA expects the throughput from Russian refineries to be more than 25% lower in 2026 compared with the previous year. Russia has, in turn, banned gasoline exports and restricted jet-fuel exports to protect domestic supplies. Consequently, combined diesel and gas oil11 exports from the Middle East and Russia were down by 75% in August compared with a year ago.12 Refiners in other nations have raised output in response to higher margins, but not enough to close the global supply gap. Unlike crude, refined products cannot be replaced quickly as refineries need spare capacity and the right crude slate. Hence, prices have risen. As of Sept. 22, 2026, US retail diesel prices were up 74% since the start of the conflict, while gasoline prices had risen 50%. Natural gas markets show a broadly similar pattern. Before the conflict, the Strait of Hormuz carried nearly one-fifth of global liquified natural gas (LNG) supplies.14 But between March and June, LNG loadings for Qatar and the United Arab Emirates were 35 billion cubic meters lower than a year earlier, while damage to LNG facilities at Qatar’s Ras Laffan complex has likely added to the strain. Increased supply from North America and Africa has partially bridged the supply gap. Nevertheless, natural gas prices have risen significantly, especially in Europe and Asia. On Sept. 23, 2026, Dutch TTF gas futures were trading 125% higher than just before the start of the Middle East conflict.15 Prices may remain elevated as nations prepare for winter. For example, demand from the European Union may increase given that current inventories are lower than a year ago. Food, too, is not off the hook Global food supply also faces multiple challenges, particularly from reduced fertilizer output. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations, up to 30% of internationally traded fertilizers usually pass through the Strait of Hormuz.17 Disruptions to shipping in the strait, therefore, appear to have reduced exports from the region. Nitrogenous fertilizer shipments from Saudi Arabia were 63% lower in the first half of 2026 than a year earlier, while exports from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates fell by 37% and 29%, respectively, according to estimates by the International Food Policy Research Institute. Saudi Arabia is also a major exporter of phosphate fertilizers, with the institute estimating a 22% drop year over year in the six months through June 2026. The closure of the strait has also disrupted shipments of sulfur, a key ingredient in manufacturing phosphate fertilizers. The immediate impact of fertilizer supply disruption has been on prices. According to the World Bank, urea prices surged by 81.5% between February and April. Prices, however, have eased since then and returned to almost pre-conflict levels due to three reasons: First, stranded Gulf shipments made their way out in June when hostilities ceased for a while. Second, producers like the United States and China ramped up exports. Finally, surging prices early in the conflict led to a drop in global demand. The same, however, cannot be said of phosphate fertilizers like diammonium phosphate, as sulfur supplies remain tight and keep prices elevated. If fertilizer supplies do not normalize, farmers may reduce dependence or shift crops, potentially affecting yields next year. These shocks may also reduce the resilience of the global food system at a time when climate-related risks (such as those from El Niño–related effects) are rising. There have also been disruptions in the Black Sea region, with strikes on storage and port infrastructure around Odesa constraining Ukraine’s ability to move its harvest to global markets.26 Together with higher energy and freight costs, these factors suggest that the global food supply chain could remain under pressure. Food prices have, therefore, edged up. The FAO food-price index rose by 6.4% between February and August. The corresponding increase in the same period last year was just 2.7%. Shipping is becoming a more challenging business In addition to energy flows, the Gulf is also a major trade hub for merchandise trade. Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, therefore, have affected not only global energy supply chains but also broader merchandise shipping—an important enabler of international trade. Renewed risks in the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, following hostilities in Yemen, have added to these pressures. According to the UK Maritime Trade Operations and the Joint Maritime Information Center, there have been 116 confirmed vessel incidents in the Middle East maritime region between March 1 and Sept. 20, 2026.28 These incidents highlight the broader risks to seaborne trade despite US-facilitated transits and a strong naval presence. Due to such incidents, risks to vessel crews and port workers have likely gone up as well. According to the International Maritime Organization, there have been 24 confirmed seafarer fatalities in 120 confirmed incidents (as of Oct. 22, 2026) in and around the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East.29 The organization’s incident-level reports also indicate that at least 53 seafarers were injured.30 These numbers help explain why shipping companies, insurers, and cargo owners continue to treat the region as a high-risk one. War-risk insurance costs have consequently risen, adding to higher freight costs. The Baltic dirty tanker index, for example, which tracks freight rates for crude tankers, is now more than four times its level a year earlier. Other freight indices also show a similar upward trend. The disruption has also encouraged greater use of ship-to-ship transfers, especially in waters off the coast of Oman. A large crude oil–carrying tanker may transit the Strait of Hormuz with its automatic identification system transponder switched off, using a US-facilitated route. Once in Omani waters, it may transfer its cargo to another vessel, which then carries it to an importing country. While this has helped some crude from the Gulf find its way to global markets, the process is costly and may increase operational risks, including collision, vessel damage, environmental harm, and reduced regulatory oversight, which have been the hallmarks of credible maritime trade. Brace for impact: Inflation and borrowing costs rise in the United States With conflicts not only hitting energy and food supply chains but wider international trade as well, it’s only natural that their impact is being felt by consumers, businesses, and governments the world over. In the United States, energy-driven inflation has added to existing price pressures. Inflation for energy goods and services was negative in January and February of this year but rose to 23.7% in May; the figure was 16.8% in August. Businesses in the country that were already facing tariff-related cost pressures are seeing production costs rise further . It is likely that they are passing on some of these costs to consumers: Durable goods inflation in August was nearly double of what it was a year ago. As price pressures rose, the Federal Reserve responded by tightening monetary policy. On Sept. 16, 2026, the Fed raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points—the first rate hike since 2023.36 In its median projections, the Federal Open Market Committee indicated the possibility of another hike this year. This marks a reversal from March, when the committee’s median quarterly projections had indicated a rate cut of 25 basis points later this year, followed by a similar cut in 2027.38 However, it’s not just the Federal Reserve that has moved toward tighter monetary policy in response to rising inflation risks. The European Central Bank has raised rates twice this year by a total of 50 basis points, and so has the Bank of Japan, pushing the country’s policy rate to its highest level in 31 years. Rising inflation and inflation expectations have likely led bond markets to reassess monetary policy stances and the fiscal health of governments. Consequently, government bond yields have risen. In the United States, the 10-year Treasury yield rose to a 19-year high on Sept. 24, 2026, while the 30-year yield is now the highest in 22 years. This could potentially raise borrowing costs for businesses and households. Interest rates for auto loans, credit card debt, and mortgages are often influenced by the 10-year Treasury yield. As Treasury yields rise, so too have consumer borrowing costs: The 30-year fixed mortgage rate, for example, was at 7.1% on Sept. 23, 2026—the highest in nearly 18 months. Rising government bond yields can also increase interest costs for the government. Net interest payments are now the third-largest spending item for the US federal government. With debt and deficit levels already high, rising borrowing costs could also limit the US government’s ability to respond to any future economic crisis. It is an issue that other governments across the developed world may also face if current geopolitical conflicts persist. Source: Deloitte 2026-11-03 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Gemini’s Suez return puts network flexibility to the test
articles.summary: The Gemini Cooperation’s latest return to the Suez Canal raises a question that goes beyond sailing distances: how much flexibility can Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd gain as they rebuild a network originally operated around the Cape of Good Hope? The partners’ decision to reroute their India–Europe IOS/ME1 service through...
articles.body: The Gemini Cooperation’s latest return to the Suez Canal raises a question that goes beyond sailing distances: how much flexibility can Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd gain as they rebuild a network originally operated around the Cape of Good Hope? The partners’ decision to reroute their India–Europe IOS/ME1 service through the Red Sea, announced on 2 November , adds another connection to a growing group of Gemini services using the shorter corridor. Yet the operational benefits will depend on more than the route itself. The carriers are simultaneously modifying service rotations and hub connections. This makes the return to Suez a test of whether shorter voyages can be translated into a more efficient and resilient network without creating new vulnerabilities if regional security conditions change. Shorter voyages do not automatically mean fewer ships The most immediate potential benefit of the Suez route is a reduction in sailing distance compared with the diversion around southern Africa. For a weekly container service, shorter voyages can reduce the number of vessels needed to maintain its frequency. The relationship is straightforward. A weekly service with a 70-day round trip requires approximately ten vessels, assuming regular departures and no additional operational allowances. If its round trip falls to 63 days, nine vessels could theoretically maintain the same frequency. This is an illustrative calculation, not a forecast for IOS/ME1. Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd have not disclosed a revised round-trip duration, the number of vessels currently assigned to the service or any planned reduction in deployment. The distinction is important because the carriers have several options. They could release capacity for other trades, retain vessels to improve schedule recovery or adjust sailing speeds and port stays. Each choice would produce a different commercial outcome. A shorter route therefore creates potential flexibility, but does not establish how the partners intend to use it. The changing role of Gemini’s hubs The network implications become clearer when IOS/ME1 is considered alongside Gemini’s wider restructuring. On 19 October, Maersk announced additional network enhancements , including a new AE18 service and changes to AE2, AE11 and AE19. These were not simply routing adjustments. AE2 is scheduled to replace its westbound Tangier call with Rotterdam, while AE11 will add Salalah westbound and replace Tangier with Port Said. The new AE18 will take over selected Tangier and Algeciras coverage previously provided by other services. This matters for IOS/ME1 because its revised rotation retains both Salalah and Tangier. The two hubs therefore remain relevant to the India–Europe connection even as other Gemini services change how they use them. The announcements suggest a redistribution of network functions rather than a uniform shift towards or away from individual ports. For example, Salalah gains an additional role in AE11 while remaining on IOS/ME1. Tangier loses certain calls on AE2 and AE11 but retains coverage through IOS/ME1 and the newly introduced AE18. These changes do not prove that either port will handle more or less cargo. Port-call patterns alone cannot establish throughput, transshipment volumes or changes in market share. They do, however, show how the partners are reorganising connections between mainline services and their hubs. The central operational question is whether the revised structure will improve connections without increasing dependence on particular transfer windows. The importance of connecting services Gemini’s hub-based model places considerable emphasis on the coordination of mainline vessels and connecting services. The shorter Suez route may help reduce time at sea, but that advantage can be weakened if cargo misses a connection or experiences delays at a transfer port. This creates a distinction between vessel transit time and end-to-end cargo delivery. A service may reach a hub earlier while offering little improvement to the customer if the onward connection remains unchanged. Conversely, a modest reduction in sailing time could have a larger commercial effect if it allows containers to meet an earlier departure. The October network changes provide evidence that Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd are working on the structure of those connections alongside their routing decisions. They do not yet provide enough information to quantify the resulting improvements. Assessing the commercial impact will require updated origin-destination schedules, connection times and actual service performance after the changes take effect. The operational cost of keeping alternatives open Security remains the principal uncertainty surrounding the transition. Both carriers have made clear that further routing decisions depend on conditions in the Red Sea. Their latest ME1 announcement maintains that vessel, crew and cargo safety will determine subsequent adjustments. That introduces a practical challenge for network planning. A service designed around Suez has different voyage durations and scheduling requirements from one routed around the Cape. If security conditions force another diversion, the carriers may need to absorb longer voyages, adjust departure schedules or introduce additional vessel capacity to preserve service frequency. Retaining spare operating capacity could make such a transition easier, but it would also limit the immediate efficiency gains available from shorter voyages. Releasing that capacity could improve utilisation while reducing the margin for responding to disruption. Neither carrier has disclosed how much contingency capacity it intends to retain. The trade-off is nevertheless central to the economics of a gradual return. The question is not simply whether Suez is shorter. It is whether the network can operate efficiently through Suez while remaining capable of responding to another interruption. What will show whether the strategy is working? The next phase should be judged through operating results rather than the number of services announced for Suez. The first measure will be actual transit times and schedule performance on IOS/ME1. The second will be the quality of connections through Salalah and Tangier as the wider Gemini changes take effect. The third will be any evidence of vessel redeployment or adjustments to service frequency. Changes in port throughput could provide additional context, although they would need to be interpreted alongside developments affecting other carriers and trades. The latest rerouting strengthens the evidence that Gemini is moving progressively towards a Suez-based network. It does not establish that the transition is complete or that the partners have already realised measurable capacity savings. For Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd, the more consequential test lies ahead: whether shorter routes, revised hub functions and contingency planning can operate together without compromising the reliability that the Gemini Cooperation is designed to deliver.

Yet the operational benefits will depend on more than the route itself.
The carriers are simultaneously modifying service rotations and hub connections.

articles.title: The Bilbao Port Authority chairs the working group to draw up a report on the FuelEU Maritime Regulation
articles.summary: In line with its strategy for sustainability and decarbonisation, the Bilbao Port Authority has chaired a working group of the European Commission’s European Sustainable Shipping Forum (ESSF), tasked with analysing the provisions relating to the supply of electricity to ships in port (OPS) under the FuelEU Maritime...
articles.body: The Bilbao Port Authority chairs the working group to draw up a report on the FuelEU Maritime Regulation in Port News 03/11/2026 In line with its strategy for sustainability and decarbonisation, the Bilbao Port Authority has chaired a working group of the European Commission’s European Sustainable Shipping Forum (ESSF), tasked with analysing the provisions relating to the supply of electricity to ships in port (OPS) under the FuelEU Maritime Regulation. The resulting report has been published by the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Mobility and Transport (DG MOVE), which has praised the work of the parties involved and the group’s coordination. In undertaking this task, The Bilbao Port Authority is strengthening its involvement in European initiatives on maritime decarbonisation and is contributing to the analysis of the regulatory framework for port electrification. The report prepared by the working group chaired by the Bilbao Port Authority has addressed the main challenges in implementing the OPS provisions of the FuelEU Maritime Regulation, and has set out the various viewpoints of different stakeholders in the maritime and port sector, all within the framework of the European regulation. It highlights that, whilst the FuelEU Maritime Regulation establishes a framework for reducing emissions from ships whilst in port, its implementation poses certain operational, technical and regulatory challenges. The document identifies aspects that may require specific clarification or adjustments, taking into account the different viewpoints of the participants involved and to help ensure the consistent and effective implementation of the legislation across the European Union. Across the various chapters of the report, the need to strike an appropriate balance between addressing genuine operational or technical difficulties and ensuring the effective deployment and use of OPS is highlighted. To this end, the report analyses various scenarios that may arise during the implementation of OPS, such as short port calls, equipment breakdowns, technical incompatibilities, unforeseen circumstances and/or price fluctuations, amongst others. The working group has also highlighted the importance not only of establishing a credible, predictable and stable framework for the use of OPS, thereby supporting the effective use of the system deployed under the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR), but also of building confidence in the significant investments being made by ports, terminal operators, electricity suppliers, shipping companies and other stakeholders. The issues addressed in this report are in line with the ongoing efforts of the Bilbao Port Authority to improve sustainability and decarbonisation at its facilities, as part of its compliance with the FuelEU Maritime Regulation. In the port itself, progress is being made in the roll-out of the OPS system, which will enable ships to connect to the onshore power grid whilst at berth, thereby removing the need for auxiliary engines and reducing emissions, noise and vibration levels. The Port Authority is also working on the gradual integration of renewable energy into its power supply model, with a view to moving towards a more sustainable and competitive port energy system. All the facilities for this service are scheduled to come into operation by the end of 2027, and they are co-funded by the Port Authority itself and by the European Commission through the CEF (Connecting Europe Facility) programme, the Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan – NextGenerationEU, and the EIB (European Investment Bank). articles.title: Aramco Targets Hormuz Bypass with East-West Pipeline Expansion
articles.summary: Saudi state oil giant Aramco is working to expand a crude pipeline that circumvents the Strait of Hormuz as the world continues to experience the biggest energy supply shock in history, CEO Amin Nasser said on Tuesday.The effective blockade of the chokepoint that links the Gulf to world markets…
articles.body: Aramco Targets Hormuz Bypass with East-West Pipeline Expansion Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 3, 2026 © chitsanupong / Adobe Stock Saudi state oil giant Aramco is working to expand a crude pipeline that circumvents the Strait of Hormuz as the world continues to experience the biggest energy supply shock in history, CEO Amin Nasser said on Tuesday. The effective blockade of the chokepoint that links the Gulf to world markets, previously a conduit for 20% of global oil supplies, has redrawn global energy flows and infrastructure investment priorities among the region's oil producers. Last month, Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said the kingdom was looking to expand its capacity to export crude by pipeline to as much as 10 million barrels per ‌day by repurposing a domestic gas pipeline and investing in its existing East-West network. "With regard to the expansion to our East-West pipeline and the additional networks that we are building, this work has already started," Nasser told analysts on a call following the company's results on Tuesday. Aramco currently has three export route options — the Gulf via the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Suez Canal. The company, which reported a more than one-third surge in third-quarter profit on Tuesday, is doing engineering work for export routes in addition to these, Nasser said. Aramco Studying Additional Storage Abroad The East-West pipeline, which has been attacked several times throughout the US-Iran war, has the capacity to carry up to 7 million barrels of oil a day. Nasser has previously described it as a critical lifeline. Nasser said until final investment decisions are made, the company will not disclose details on the new export routes being worked on. The impact of the crisis extends far beyond the energy market, Nasser said earlier in a statement to Reuters. Aramco is also exploring additional storage capacity abroad, he said. "Higher transportation costs, fertiliser shortages, and impacts on food and consumer goods are feeding into inflationary pressures across the global economy," he said. More than 130 attacks on tankers have been reported so far during the Iran conflict, mainly against very large crude carriers, causing freight rates to surge more than 15 times from a year ago, Nasser said. VLCCs can carry 2 million barrels of oil. "Demand fundamentals remain strong and the world cannot afford to plan its energy future around short-term market conditions. We remain ready to rapidly ramp up production when the situation calls for it," Nasser said. articles.body: Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan have signed two agreements to develop transport and logistics connections across the Caspian Sea, including a proposed ferry system and an intermodal cargo terminal at the Port of Baku. The agreements were signed during a meeting between Kazakhstan’s sovereign wealth fund Samruk-Kazyna and Azerbaijan’s state-owned AZCON Holding on 2 November 2026. The initiatives aim to strengthen maritime and rail connectivity along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, also known as the Middle Corridor. New Caspian ferry system and intermodal terminal Under the first agreement, Samruk-Kazyna and AZCON Holding will cooperate on the proposed Caspian Bridge ferry system, also referred to as the Super Ferry project. The agreement establishes the main principles and areas of cooperation for preparing and developing the project. However, the organisations have not announced a construction timetable, vessel specifications or an investment value. Meanwhile, Kazakhstan Temir Zholy and Azerbaijan Railways signed a term sheet outlining the main conditions for establishing an intermodal cargo terminal and a joint venture. According to AZCON Holding, the proposed terminal would be located within the Baku International Sea Trade Port. The project is intended to support container and other cargo movements, with particular emphasis on the Middle Corridor. By linking maritime transport across the Caspian Sea with rail infrastructure, the proposed developments could strengthen cargo connections between Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan. The two countries are seeking to improve transport capacity and coordination along the route, which connects Asian and European markets through the Caspian region. In addition, representatives of Samruk-Kazyna and AZCON discussed potential cooperation in dredging, marine infrastructure and corporate governance. The discussions also covered opportunities for closer coordination between companies within the two state-owned groups. Neither organisation disclosed the expected cargo-handling capacity of the proposed terminal or a timetable for the ferry system. The agreements represent an initial framework for further project development rather than confirmation that construction or commercial operations have begun.

articles.title: Efficiency and the new economics of shipping’s decarbonisation
articles.summary: Oskar Levander from Kongsberg Maritime writes for Splash today. For almost two decades, efficiency has been routine good practice in shipping. Owners have cut fuel burn and improved hull and propeller performance. These useful measures were often treated in isolation as cost control. However, this approach no longer...
articles.body: Contributions Environment Operations Efficiency and the new economics of shipping’s decarbonisation Splash November 3, 2026 0 158 2 minutes read Kongsberg Maritime Kongsberg Maritime Oskar Levander from Kongsberg Maritime writes for Splash today. For almost two decades, efficiency has been routine good practice in shipping. Owners have cut fuel burn and improved hull and propeller performance. These useful measures were often treated in isolation as cost control. However, this approach no longer fits the complexity facing the sector, nor the larger question of how to pay for decarbonisation. Efficiency can help fund it. The EU ETS brought shipping into carbon pricing in 2024. It covers all intra-EU emissions and half of emissions on voyages in and out of EU ports. FuelEU Maritime penalises fuels that miss a GHG intensity target that tightens with each compliance period. The IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework would apply similar logic to the global fleet: a worldwide fuel-intensity standard backed by emissions pricing. Ships that beat the target could earn tradeable credits; those that fall short would pay into an IMO fund. Member states are due to vote on adoption in December 2026. If adopted, rules could take effect from 2028. These regulations give efficiency and clean energy sources a new value. It can earn money to fund new fuels and supporting technology. For example, under EU ETS, every tonne of CO2 a vessel does not emit is an allowance the owner does not have to buy or surrender. As free allocation to shipping is phased out, a container ship saving several thousand tonnes of CO2 a year avoids a large compliance cost before any fuel savings are considered. Many owners have yet to catch up. Payback calculations based on fuel savings alone now understate the return. Hull optimisation, wind assistance, propulsion upgrades, heat recovery and digital energy management each deliver lower fuel costs, avoided ETS allowances, lower FuelEU compliance costs, and, for fleets with verified data, premiums from charterers and green finance providers. A recent Kongsberg Maritime study shows the change that is possible. The Kamsarmax design combines hull and propulsion optimisation, integrated energy management and wind assistance on long open-sea routes. Modelled against a conventional Kamsarmax on a similar trade, it cuts fuel use by more than 40%, and by over half on the most wind-favourable routes. Every tonne of fuel saved on European trades is a tonne less exposed to EU ETS, and it reduces the vessel’s overall FuelEU compliance costs. Additionally, the wind assistance technologies also earn the vessel a FuelEU reward factor. Owners who still judge efficiency on fuel cost alone are underestimating the return. A project that looked like a seven-year payback in 2021 could instead be a three-year payback in 2026, before any premium from a greener charter rate or better finance terms is realised. While carbon prices are volatile, banking on future compliance savings can be risky. The caution is fair, but EU carbon prices have risen as free allowances are withdrawn. Even at a modest price, the saving from lower fuel burn over a vessel’s two- or three-decade working life can outweigh the risk of a weaker carbon market. Waiting for price certainty means waiting for something that will never come. Efficiency is also fuel agnostic. Whether ships run on methanol, ammonia, bio-LNG, hydrogen derivatives or a mix, a vessel that needs less energy will be cheaper to run. With rules still being written and the future remaining uncertain, that flexibility is worth a great deal. Decarbonisation is as much a balance-sheet problem as an engineering one. Efficiency is the most practical lever owners have. Those who combine small gains, prove them with verified data, and put the savings back into the transition can fund their way through the next decade. articles.body: Exploration & Production November 3, 2026 · 5 minutes ago Vår Energi comes up dry in the North Sea Vår Energi’s drilling operations with COSL Drilling Europe’s rig in the Norwegian sector of the North Sea have not yielded hydrocarbons. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email COSL Pioneer rig Source: COSL Drilling Europe Norwegian oil and gas player Vår Energi and its partners, Equinor, DNO Norge, and Petoro, have drilled a wildcat well on the Norwegian Continental Shelf (NCS), which ended up being dry. The wildcat well 25/8-24 S , also known as the Jotun Deep prospect, was drilled in production license 1203, 20 kilometers northwest of the Ringhorne installation and 190 kilometers west of Stavanger, as the first well drilled in this license, which was awarded in March 2024 (APA 2023). The licensees in production license 1203 are Vår Energi (operator), Equinor, DNO, and Petoro. This well was drilled by the COSL Pioneer rig. The well was drilled to a vertical depth of 3,417 meters below sea level and was terminated in what, so far, is presumed to be the Smith Bank Formation. While the well's primary exploration target was to prove petroleum in the Statfjord Formation in the Late Triassic to Early Jurassic, the secondary exploration target was to prove petroleum in the Skagerrak Formation in the Late Triassic, in addition to proving petroleum in underlying layers. The well 25/8-24 S encountered a reservoir in the upper Statfjord Formation with a total thickness of 81 meters, 64 meters of which were sandstone with good reservoir quality. The reservoir was aquiferous. The lower Statfjord Formation was encountered with a total thickness of 53 meters, 23 meters of which were sandstone with good reservoir quality. The reservoir was aquiferous. In the secondary exploration target, the well encountered the Skagerrak Formation with a total thickness of 161 meters. The formation contains two thicker sandstone layers with moderate reservoir properties, in addition to multiple thin sandstone layers with poor reservoir properties. The reservoir was aquiferous. Under the Skagerrak Formation, the well encountered rocks with poor reservoir quality, most likely the Smith Bank Formation in the Early to Middle Triassic. According to the Norwegian Offshore Directorate, weak hydrocarbon indications in the potential Smith Bank Formation cannot be ruled out. The well was not formation-tested, but extensive volumes of data were collected. The water depth at the site is 127 meters, and the well has been permanently plugged and abandoned. articles.title: Black Sea Maritime War Spreads as NATO Faces Growing Security Threat
articles.summary: After seven strikes on cargo ships near NATO members Romania and Bulgaria last month, the US-led military alliance said it would deploy maritime patrol aircraft, radars and drones to bolster its eastern flank in the Black Sea.Three days later…
articles.body: Black Sea Maritime War Spreads as NATO Faces Growing Security Threat Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 3, 2026 © olinchuk / Adobe Stock After seven strikes on cargo ships near NATO members Romania and Bulgaria last month, the US-led military alliance said it would deploy maritime patrol aircraft, radars and drones to bolster its eastern flank in the Black Sea. Three days later, on October 23, another ship was struck just outside Romanian waters. And last week a Greek container ship was sunk by naval drones in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. Unabating attacks show how the escalating maritime war between Russia and Ukraine is expanding into a major challenge for NATO in the Black Sea that has left littoral member states such as Romania and Bulgaria exposed. Military analysts said they had little doubt that these were Russian attacks. A naval drone seen on video of the last strike resembled a Russian variant, according to shipping security firm Ambrey. "I think it's undeniably an escalation," said Sidharth Kaushal, a senior fellow at the London-based RUSI think-tank. Russia denies targeting Ukraine's neighbours with drones and says that European governments are the ones escalating the war in Ukraine by supplying military aid. Russia's defence ministry did not respond to a request for comment for this article. Analyst Says Russia Is Testing Red Lines Many of the ships hit in October were anchored near or sailing to or from a key Romanian canal used by Ukraine for exports. One was in Romanian territorial waters, while the other eight were in its or Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. Iulia Joja, director of the Black Sea programme for the Washington-based Middle East Institute think-tank, said Russia's attacks were taking into account the West's aversion to escalation. "This is about testing these red lines, with full awareness that we will do everything possible to take the most minimal measures," Joja said, drawing a comparison with Russian drone incursions into NATO airspace in recent years. A NATO official said Russian actions aimed at dissuading NATO allies from supporting Ukraine were a serious security threat and that the alliance's commitment to defending all its members, including those on the Black Sea, was "ironclad". The official said there was a clear need for cost-effective counter-drone capabilities, but that the alliance had already committed to investing more than $40 billion in counter-drone capabilities in the next five years. Black Sea Is Crucial Waterway For Romania, the Black Sea is a crucial waterway for trade and home to its offshore Neptun Deep project that will make it the European Union's largest gas producer next year. Neptun Deep was approached by a naval drone in August. Bucharest has accused Russia of "systematic" strikes on civilian ships but stopped short of attributing individual attacks, citing the need for forensic evidence. Sofia has not blamed Russia, but said some of the attacks seem to benefit it. The strikes come at a time when Washington is reassessing its military presence in Europe as it focuses on China. The US withdrew 1,000 troops from Romania last year. "It's a moment in the transatlantic relationship that Putin likely wants to use," said a senior Romanian official. "The EU and NATO's attention is important and their forces are currently focusing towards the north and the Baltics." While NATO has reinforced its "enhanced forward presence" for the Baltics and Poland, Joja said it had not done the same in Romania despite Bucharest's requests. "Brussels and Washington still don't seem to have decided whether the Black Sea is fully part of the NATO commitment." The Romanian official highlighted Romania's pressing need for surface-to-air interceptors and radar systems to counter threats. Joja said the limited availability of cheap interceptor weapons, exacerbated by the war in Iran, was a central problem for the West. Nearly 400 Vessels Hit in Past Year The surge in strikes on Black Sea shipping has strangled a major conduit for exports of grain and oil used by Russia and Ukraine. The two sides hit 317 merchant and other vessels in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov between May and October, a more than fourfold rise on the 74 vessels they struck in the previous half-year, according to Tomas Alexa, a senior analyst at Ambrey Analytics. The tempo of attacks has fluctuated ahead of the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion in February. Ukraine carried out 137 attacks on ships compared with 92 Russian ones in the third quarter, while in October, Russia hit 38 compared with 5 Ukrainian strikes, Ambrey said. Grain Exports from Ukraine and Russia Slump Ports have been battered and exports have shrivelled, forcing Russia and Ukraine to seek alternative export routes. Russia exported just 0.3 million metric tons of grain in September through the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, down from 4.74 million metric tons in the same month last year, according to Russian export data seen by Reuters. Ukraine suspended operations at its Black Sea ports in late July due to Russian attacks, prompting it to divert volumes to river ports on the Danube and onwards through Romania's Sulina Canal and southwards through Romania's section of the Black Sea. Even with this alternative route, Ukraine's port exports of grain slumped to 0.81 million metric tons in September compared with 2.1 million in September last year, government data showed. Further reducing these volumes remains Russia's primary goal with testing NATO as the secondary objective, said Andriy Ryzhenko, a naval analyst and former senior Ukrainian naval officer. Zelenskiy Warns of Food Crisis Last week's attack took place as the defence ministers and military chiefs of Romania, Bulgaria and fellow NATO littoral state Turkey met in Sofia to discuss the situation. The defence minister of Turkey, which is waiting for a response from Moscow and Kyiv on a narrow maritime ceasefire proposal, used the meeting to warn Russia and Ukraine against further attacks. Turkey controls the transit of warships through the Bosphorus and Dardanelles under the Montreux Convention. Several countries, including Egypt, Turkey and India, have pushed for maritime ceasefires to avert fallout from the disruption of shipping at a time when global fuel and grain prices have soared. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday there was growing international interest in a limited ceasefire. Russia has rejected the idea of a narrow maritime ceasefire that it says would provide respite to Kyiv. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy has sounded the alarm. "Everyone is talking about diesel and forgetting about grain. In a month or two, everyone will start talking about an agricultural crisis," he said last month. (Reuters - Reporting by Tom Balmforth in London and Luiza Ilie in Bucharest; Additional reporting by Pavel Polityuk, Gergely Szakacs, Gleb Stolyarov, Edward Carron and Michael Jones; Editing by Mike Collett-White and Alison Williams)

articles.body: Descartes Systems Group has integrated its MacroPoint Advanced Ocean Visibility solution with two SAP transportation platforms, providing shippers with improved container tracking and multimodal shipment visibility. The integration connects Descartes MacroPoint with SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration and SAP Business Network Global Track and Trace through the Descartes Global Logistics Network (GLN). As a result, customers can access ocean shipment information directly within their existing SAP systems. The connection aims to simplify cargo monitoring and improve coordination across international supply chains. Enhanced container visibility across transport networks The integrated solution provides near real-time tracking of containers throughout their journeys. It covers key shipping milestones, including vessel departures, arrivals, loading operations and container gate movements. In addition, the platform combines ocean freight information with road transport visibility. This allows shippers to monitor different stages of cargo movements through a more consistent digital environment. The integration uses standardised application programming interfaces (APIs) and harmonised data models to exchange shipment information between the platforms. According to Descartes, the system has undergone testing to verify reliable data exchange, accurate milestone tracking and support for complex shipping operations. Dan Cicerchi, Executive Vice President of Corporate and Operations Development at Descartes, said the integration will help companies respond more effectively to supply chain disruptions. The new connection builds on Descartes’ existing integration with SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration, which already supports logistics processes such as carrier bookings. Meanwhile, the expanded functionality allows ocean tracking information to become part of broader transportation planning and execution workflows. Descartes MacroPoint Advanced Ocean Visibility is now available through the SAP Store. The company has not disclosed how many customers are currently using the new integration.

articles.title: Singapore VLSFO back above $1,000 for first time since March
articles.summary: The cost of fuelling ships has climbed back above $1,000 a tonne in Singapore for the first time since March, as the prolonged Iran conflict continues to drive up bunker bills across the global merchant fleet. Data from Ship & Bunker show very low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO) broke through the $1,000 threshold on October …
articles.body: Asia Bunkering Europe Middle East Singapore VLSFO back above $1,000 for first time since March Sam Chambers November 3, 2026 0 394 1 minute read The cost of fuelling ships has climbed back above $1,000 a tonne in Singapore for the first time since March, as the prolonged Iran conflict continues to drive up bunker bills across the global merchant fleet. Data from Ship & Bunker show very low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO) broke through the $1,000 threshold on October 28, reaching $1,000.50 a tonne. Prices subsequently climbed to $1,019.50 on Friday before easing to $1,003.50 on Monday. High sulphur fuel oil (HSFO) was assessed at $898.50 a tonne on Monday, while marine gasoil stood at $1,263. The figures illustrate the extraordinary transformation of the bunker market since the US-Israeli strikes on Iran began on February 28. Ship & Bunker data show Singapore VLSFO was trading at $521.50 a tonne immediately before the conflict. The fuel has since increased by more than 92%, having reached a peak of $1,120.50 on March 13. For a ship taking on 3,000 tonnes of VLSFO, the current bunker bill is approximately $3m, compared with $1.56m before the war, an additional $1.45m for a single stem. Scrubber-equipped vessels retain a significant advantage, with the Singapore VLSFO-HSFO spread currently standing at $105 a tonne. However, the absolute cost of burning either fuel has escalated dramatically. The price surge is also affecting alternative fuels. According to bunker pricing specialist ENGINE, LNG bunkers in Singapore reached $1,939 a tonne on Monday, up $74 over the previous week. Rotterdam LNG prices climbed $97 to $1,873, reflecting tighter European gas markets and continuing Middle Eastern disruption. LNG and oil-based bunker prices are not directly comparable by weight because of their different energy content. Regional bunker price disparities are substantial. Ship & Bunker assessed Rotterdam VLSFO at $763.50 a tonne on Monday, around $240 below Singapore, while Fujairah was quoted at $991.50. The Hormuz crisis has also complicated bunker procurement, with fuel shortages and extended delivery lead times forcing vessels to reconsider where and when they refuel. articles.title: October deluge brings Panama Canal lake levels back towards normal
articles.summary: A surprisingly wet October has brought much-needed relief to the Panama Canal, with Gatun Lake recovering to near its historical average despite warnings that a powerful El Niño could trigger another prolonged drought. New research from Ursa Shipbrokers, drawing on Panama Canal Authority data, shows Gatun Lake...
articles.body: Americas Containers Dry Cargo Gas Operations Tankers October deluge brings Panama Canal lake levels back towards normal Sam Chambers November 3, 2026 0 881 1 minute read Monjasa Monjasa A surprisingly wet October has brought much-needed relief to the Panama Canal, with Gatun Lake recovering to near its historical average despite warnings that a powerful El Niño could trigger another prolonged drought. New research from Ursa Shipbrokers, drawing on Panama Canal Authority data, shows Gatun Lake averaged 85.80 ft (26.15 m) over the first 30 days of October, just 0.15 ft below its historical October average. The recovery is particularly striking compared with 2023, when severe drought crippled canal operations. October’s average was 6.04 ft higher than the corresponding month three years ago. The turnaround follows an unusually prolonged decline in lake levels, which continued until August this year rather than bottoming out in May, as is normally the case. Rainfall statistics underline the improvement. Data compiled from the canal authority’s meteorological stations show 303.3 mm of rain fell across the watershed between October 1 and 29, 8.4% above the 30-year average and 83.6% more than during the same period in drought-stricken 2023. By October 29, Gatun Lake’s daily level had reached 86.56 ft, up from an August low of 83.80 ft. Improved conditions have allowed the canal authority to reverse some restrictions. From October 15, daily transit availability increased to 33 vessels, while the maximum neopanamax draft was raised to 49 ft. The authority has also reinstated last-minute reservations for panamax vessels. Nevertheless, the drought threat has not disappeared. Rainfall since May remains almost 20% below average, following a particularly dry summer when watershed inflows were 44% below normal. With El Niño forecast to persist into 2027, the coming dry season will test whether October’s welcome soaking has provided sufficient protection against another round of restrictions. During his leadership, AD Ports Group developed from a local port operator into an international business with activities spanning ports, shipping, logistics and industrial infrastructure. The group currently operates 40 terminals and maintains a presence in more than 50 countries across five continents. articles.body: Asia Dry Cargo Operations Press Releases Tankers Tech Splash Singapore unveils 2027 agenda with three new sessions tackling shipping’s biggest challenges Splash November 3, 2026 0 473 2 minutes read Splash Singapore has unveiled the agenda for its 2027 edition, introducing three new sessions examining crewing, operational efficiency and maritime investment alongside traditional tanker and dry bulk market outlooks. The conference returns to the Stamford Ballroom at Raffles City Convention Centre on Thursday, September 23, 2027, building on the success of its inaugural edition earlier this year. Discounted room rates at the adjacent five-star Fairmont Hotel are also on offer. Organised by the team behind Splash and Geneva Dry, the event retains its established formula: no presentations, no slides and no selling, just unscripted debate between some of shipping’s most influential decision-makers. Three new sessions will make their debut next September. Crewing In The Digital Age will explore how technology is transforming the recruitment, training, retention and welfare of seafarers. From artificial intelligence and digital platforms to onboard connectivity and changing crew expectations, the discussion will examine how shipowners and managers can attract and retain talent while improving operational performance.’ The Business Of Efficiency will tackle one of shipping’s most pressing commercial questions: where can owners genuinely improve performance and profitability? From new technologies and alternative fuels to emissions reduction and operational improvements, panellists will debate which investments deliver measurable returns and which risk becoming expensive distractions. The three new sessions get right to the heart of the decisions shipping companies are making every day Money & Ships brings maritime finance and investment decisions into the spotlight. Taking into account freight markets, the global orderbook, access to capital, fuel choices and listed share performance, the session will ask where shipping’s next investment opportunities lie and whether today’s asset prices can be justified. Grant Rowles, Splash Singapore co-founder, said the refreshed programme reflects the industry’s changing priorities. “We had a tremendous response to our first Splash Singapore, and we’re determined to make the second edition even more valuable. The three new sessions get right to the heart of the decisions shipping companies are making every day: finding and retaining good people, making their operations more efficient and deciding where to invest their money. “We want an agenda that appeals to shipowners, managers, charterers, financiers and technology companies alike, with enough time throughout the day for the networking and business discussions that make these gatherings so worthwhile.” The conference will once again open with The Big Issues session, moderated by Splash editor and co-founder Sam Chambers, providing a high-level assessment of geopolitics, shipping demand, regulation, fuels and technology. Dedicated Tanker Market Outlook and Dry Bulk Market Outlook sessions will also return, completing a six-session programme designed to give delegates a comprehensive view of the industry’s prospects. Chambers said the new format builds on lessons from this year’s event. “Shipping has no shortage of conferences discussing technology or decarbonisation in broad terms. We want to get much more specific. What is technology actually delivering? How do you solve the crewing challenge? Where should shipowners be putting their capital when asset values are so high and the geopolitical outlook remains so unpredictable? These are the conversations that matter. Our aim is to bring together people who have strong opinions, real experience and a willingness to challenge one another.” The event builds on the team’s long-running Maritime CEO Forum series in Singapore and Monaco, together with the Geneva Dry commodities shipping conference. articles.body: Europe Greater China Operations Grimaldi lines up 10 car carrier newbuilds in China Adis Ajdin November 3, 2026 0 341 1 minute read Grimaldi Grimaldi Italian shipping group Grimaldi is lining up another 10 car carriers at Chinese shipyards, including a series of 11,000 ceu vessels that would become the largest in its fleet. The Naples-based owner has signed letters of intent with China Merchants for five next-generation 10,000 ceu pure car and truck carriers (PCTCs) and with CSSC’s Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI) for another five ships of 11,000 ceu each. Both designs will have additional capacity for containers and other rolling cargo, extending their capabilities beyond conventional vehicle transportation. The Emanuele Grimaldi-led owner confirmed the agreements, saying the projects would now move from preliminary design to engineering, a process expected to take around six months. Deliveries are targeted for 2030 and 2031. The agreements have yet to translate into firm shipbuilding contracts, with no pricing disclosed for the proposed vessels. The latest move builds on Grimaldi’s extensive car carrier expansion in China. In 2022 and 2023, the group amassed an orderbook of 17 ammonia-ready PCTCs (pictured), comprising 10 ships at China Merchants and seven at CSSC-affiliated yards. The owner has since been taking larger ships into its fleet, most recently the 9,800 ceu Grande Pacifico and Grande Egitto , built by China Merchants Heavy Industries Jiangsu. The pair entered service in August and September this year, becoming the largest car carriers in the group’s fleet. The proposed 11,000 ceu series would take Grimaldi another step up in vessel size, while adding greater flexibility to carry a combination of vehicles, containers and other roro cargo. The car carrier projects form part of a wider fleet investment programme valued at more than €4bn ($4.5bn). Grimaldi has also commissioned a tenth ropax ferry at China Merchants Jinling Shipyard in Weihai for its Spanish subsidiary Trasmed, involving an investment of €160m ($179m). The ship will join nine ferries ordered at the yard in April 2025 for Grimaldi’s Mediterranean and Baltic operations. Meanwhile, the group is in advanced negotiations with South Korea’s HD Hyundai and China’s China Merchants and GSI over a new series of G6-class conro vessels, although firm contracts have yet to be announced.
